items.stem: In an essay on the reading of poetry the author wrote: "Whoever believes that a reader can draw out everything a poem holds by direct encounter alone, with no prior acquaintance with the tradition in which it was written, assumes that in the meeting between reader and poem the reader is always a passive recipient — a kind of blank surface on which the poem imprints itself without any participation of his own in the act of taking it in. One hardly needs the apparatus of philosophy to see the error of this conception." Which of the following claims best expresses the conception the author of the passage himself holds?
options: The reading of a poem demands the active participation of the reader, and that participation rests on what he already knows of the tradition
A reader who comes to a poem without prior acquaintance with its tradition will draw out of it more than a reader whose knowledge stands between him and the poem
If the reader were merely a passive recipient, the writing of poetry would be a pointless act, since nothing of the poem would reach him
The complete taking-in of a poem depends on the reader's having taken part in its composition, and is therefore beyond anyone who was not present at its writing
items.explanation: The author faults the belief for assuming a passive reader; his own view is the negation — an active reader — and the belief he rejects ties that activity to prior acquaintance, so his view retains it. (2) reverses him; (3) draws a consequence he never draws; (4) turns "participation in taking it in" into participation in writing.
items.trust: derived-from-real-exam; 27 of 420 spot-checked against NITE keys, all correct

items.stem: The first cell of a living organism, formed at fertilization, is called a zygote. Compared with the typical cells of the body it will become, the zygote is enormous — so large that it can be seen without a microscope. In the hours after fertilization it divides, and its daughter cells divide again, and so on through many rounds; but during these early divisions the cells do not feed and do not grow between one division and the next, so that from a single cell of great size there results, within a few days, a cluster of several thousand cells of the size characteristic of most cells in the body. Based on the passage, during the early divisions —
options: the zygote divides into daughter cells each of which is equal to it in size, until the cluster reaches its final number
a rapid succession of divisions takes place, in which each division produces cells smaller than the cell that divided
the zygote divides into two cells whose size is already that of most cells in the body, and these then multiply without further change in size
a single large cell splits at one moment into several thousand cells of the characteristic size
items.explanation: No growth between divisions and a fixed total mass mean each division halves the size; (1) would require growth, (3) puts the whole reduction into the first division, and (4) denies the succession the passage describes.
items.trust: derived-from-real-exam; 27 of 420 spot-checked against NITE keys, all correct

items.stem: In an essay on the carpenter-builders of the old Baltic towns it was written: "That many of the timber houses still standing along those harbors were designed by a single master, Anders Holm, is known today to a handful of scholars. Such is the fate of buildings that a town adopts as its own: they are lived in, repaired, copied by the neighbors and passed from generation to generation as simply 'the houses of the harbor,' while the name of the man who first drew them is forgotten; no one asks who designed them, as though they had grown from the place like the trees. This was the fate of the finest of the vernacular builders — those whose houses answered the needs and the taste of the town so exactly that nothing in them looked like the invention of an individual mind." What is the central idea of the author's words?
options: Holm's houses spread along the harbors because they answered the town's needs and taste more exactly than the houses of the trained architects of his day
The reason Holm's houses were copied more and more widely, even as his name was forgotten, is that the copyists preserved the skill of the original designer in their imitations
The fact that Holm's authorship is known to so few is what allowed his houses to be regarded as truly belonging to the town, and so to be preserved
Precisely because Holm excelled at his craft he received no recognition for it — for the best vernacular building does not look like the work of a designer at all
items.explanation: The passage's turn is that perfection in the vernacular manner erases the author: the houses seemed to have grown from the place. (1) explains the spread but not the forgetting; (2) inverts what the copyists preserved into what the passage says was lost; (3) makes the obscurity the cause of the belonging rather than its consequence.
items.trust: derived-from-real-exam; 27 of 420 spot-checked against NITE keys, all correct

items.stem: Everyone agrees that there is a close bond between music and mathematics — not only are the intervals of the scale described by ratios of whole numbers, but more than once a discovery about the structure of music has prompted a development in mathematics. Few, however, notice that this bond is not self-evident and is indeed surprising: music addresses itself to the ear and to feeling, and its material is sound, which exists only in time, whereas mathematics deals with abstract objects that exist in no time and address themselves to no sense. The closeness between the two therefore raises philosophical questions about the relation between what is felt and what is thought. According to the passage, why is the bond between music and mathematics surprising?
options: Because it is a bond between an art and a science, and the questions it raises are therefore philosophical rather than musical or mathematical
Because the objects the two disciplines deal with are of entirely different kinds, and would seem to have nothing to do with each other
Because it reveals that the abstract objects of mathematics are in fact grasped by the senses, like sounds
Because music does not merely rest on mathematics but has also influenced its development
items.explanation: The passage grounds the surprise in the difference of kind — sound in time and felt, against abstract objects outside time and thought. (1) describes the consequence of the surprise, not its cause; (3) invents a conclusion the passage does not draw; (4) is part of the agreed bond, not of what is surprising about it.
items.trust: derived-from-real-exam; 27 of 420 spot-checked against NITE keys, all correct

items.stem: The best-known painting of the Flemish master Van Roon was called in its own day "The Wedding at the Mill." Its present name, "The Mourners," was given to it only at the end of the eighteenth century, some hundred and fifty years after it was painted, on account of the somber appearance it had acquired under the layers of soot and darkened varnish that had settled on it. After the painting was cleaned in the twentieth century it became clear that it was painted in the bright manner of its period and depicts, as its original name says, a celebration. Which of the following claims emerges from the passage regarding the name "The Mourners"?
options: Once the painting had been cleaned, the name was abandoned and the original name restored
Until the middle of the twentieth century it was believed that the painting did not depict the scene its original name described, and only the cleaning showed that it did
The name was given to the painting in order to describe the poor condition into which it had fallen under the soot
The name originated in an error about the nature of the scene depicted — an error that came to light only when the layers of soot were removed
items.explanation: (1) is not stated — the present name is still in use; (2) overstates a name into a belief held by everyone; (3) makes the name a description of the canvas's state rather than of an imagined scene.
items.trust: derived-from-real-exam; 27 of 420 spot-checked against NITE keys, all correct

items.stem: It is usual to distinguish between rust caused by moisture and rust caused by salt, but in many cases the two act on the same metal at once. Such combined corrosion is especially severe, since the moisture and the salt intensify each other's action, and not only because each of them attacks the metal on its own: the salt dissolves in the moisture and carries an electric current that speeds the reaction, and the moisture spreads the salt into cracks it could not reach when dry; moreover, the salt breaks down the protective film that a moist surface would otherwise form, so that the metal loses the defense it would have had against moisture alone. Which of the following is NOT given in the passage as a reason why combined corrosion is more severe than corrosion by moisture alone?
options: The salt destroys the protective film that would have formed on the moist metal
The salt attacks the metal faster in the presence of moisture than the moisture does on its own
The moisture carries the salt into places it could not otherwise reach
The dissolved salt conducts a current that speeds the reaction
items.explanation: The passage compares combined corrosion with each agent acting alone, but never says the salt's own attack is faster than the moisture's; (1), (3) and (4) are each stated.
items.trust: derived-from-real-exam; 27 of 420 spot-checked against NITE keys, all correct

items.stem: Researchers at the space agency report that there may be water beneath the surface of the moon Thessa. An instrument aboard the probe that passed the moon recorded, over its northern plain, an unusually low count of a certain kind of radiation — a finding that points to the presence of hydrogen, since hydrogen absorbs radiation of this kind, and hydrogen is one of the two elements of which water is composed. The researchers nevertheless hold that if there is water on Thessa, it is in the form of ice. Which of the following claims follows from the passage?
options: Where there is no water on Thessa, the count of the radiation is probably low
The chance that there is liquid water on the northern plain is greater than the chance that there is ice
Where the count of the radiation is high, there is probably water beneath the surface
The chance that there is ice on the northern plain is smaller than the chance that there is hydrogen there
items.explanation: Hydrogen is what the low count indicates; water requires hydrogen and more, and ice is the form the researchers think any water would take — so ice is the less likely of the two. (1) and (3) reverse the indicator; (2) contradicts the researchers' view.
items.trust: derived-from-real-exam; 27 of 420 spot-checked against NITE keys, all correct

items.stem: One of the central factors that hastened the development of alternative methods of assessing pupils in schools is the view that the capacity of the traditional method — the written examination at the end of a course — to reflect the knowledge and the skills it purports to measure is not high. Which of the following claims is contained in the idea expressed above?
options: The fact that the traditional method ranks pupils according to their knowledge is one of the main reasons for the development of alternative methods
The alternative methods of assessment arose out of the view that the traditional method reflects what pupils know and can do only to a limited degree
The traditional method of assessment reflects pupils' knowledge better than it reflects their skills
Since the alternative methods were developed, the traditional method has been found to reflect knowledge less well than it did before
items.explanation: (1) attributes the development to a feature the passage does not criticize; (3) splits knowledge from skills where the passage pairs them; (4) adds a change over time the passage does not describe.
items.trust: derived-from-real-exam; 27 of 420 spot-checked against NITE keys, all correct

items.stem: The planetary scientist Dr. Karin Vale said: "The moon Callas is sheathed in ice several kilometers thick, but in recent images its surface shows streaks of a rust-colored material that is certainly not ice. Plumes of warm water rising from the depths are what carry this material up through cracks in the ice. If our laboratory tests hold — and the material is indeed salt of the kind left behind by evaporating sea water — then the ocean hidden beneath the ice is in contact with rock, and is enriched with the minerals that life, as on Earth, would require." Which of the following claims does Dr. Vale present as a fact?
options: The rust-colored material on the surface of Callas is sea salt
The rust-colored material reaches the surface with water from the depths
The minerals in the hidden ocean are sufficient for life
The hidden ocean is in contact with rock
items.explanation: Only the plumes are stated outright; (1), (3) and (4) all sit inside the conditional "if our tests hold."
items.trust: derived-from-real-exam; 27 of 420 spot-checked against NITE keys, all correct

items.stem: Chemists have recently developed a way of recycling the plastic known as PET by breaking down the chemical bonds between the molecules of which it is built. Many people suppose that products made of this plastic are easy to recycle, since most drink bottles are made of it and it is well known that bottles can be recycled without difficulty. In fact, bottles are recycled mechanically — they are ground into small flakes from which new products can be molded — and most other products made of PET cannot be recycled in this way, because the purity the material retains after mechanical recycling is not high enough for them. Hence the great importance the chemists attach to their discovery. Which of the following claims does NOT follow from the passage?
options: The mechanical recycling of drink bottles is a comparatively simple process
Until the new discovery, most products made of PET could not be recycled at all
Chemical recycling breaks the material into smaller units than those produced by mechanical recycling
Thanks to the new discovery, most products made of PET can now be recycled in the same way that bottles have been recycled until now
items.explanation: The new way is chemical; the bottles' way is mechanical, and the passage says most products cannot be recycled by it. (1), (2) and (3) each follow.
items.trust: derived-from-real-exam; 27 of 420 spot-checked against NITE keys, all correct

items.stem: In recent years the share of people under the age of twenty in the population of the country has fallen, but the country's situation still differs from that of several European countries, in which the number of pupils in the school system has fallen. ____. Which of the following sentences best completes the passage?
options: In Europe, by contrast, the share of people under twenty has also fallen, while the share of the elderly has risen
According to some estimates, the fall in the share of pupils is small
In one European country — Romania — the trend has even reversed itself
In this country the total number of pupils is still growing, even if not in every sector
items.explanation: The contrast the passage sets up — a falling share but not a falling number — needs a sentence that states the second half. (1) describes Europe rather than the country; (2) and (3) are aside from the contrast.
items.trust: derived-from-real-exam; 27 of 420 spot-checked against NITE keys, all correct

items.stem: The historian Laurence Stone wrote: "In the 1930s many historians turned their backs on the tradition of narrative history in favor of what they took to be the ideal way of presenting the past. The reason was, first and foremost, a widely held and only partly justified supposition: that a simple account, concentrated on more or less chronological answers to 'what' and 'how,' contributes little to constructing an answer to 'why.'" According to the passage, what is Stone's position on the writing of history?
options: Narrative history is certainly able to shed light on the causes of events, though within limits
The purpose of historical writing is the chronological description of events, and not the discovery of their causes
There is no basis for the claim that narrative history concentrates on description rather than on causes
Historical writing that answers the questions "what" and "how" is unable to provide answers to the question "why"
items.explanation: "Only partly justified" is Stone's judgment on the supposition; if it is partly wrong, narrative history does contribute to "why" — but partly right, so within limits. (4) is the supposition itself; (2) and (3) go further than Stone in opposite directions.
items.trust: derived-from-real-exam; 27 of 420 spot-checked against NITE keys, all correct

items.stem: A newspaper reported that the consumers' council recommends buying at the "Everyday" supermarket chain, since a survey among thousands of shoppers found it to be the cheapest chain in the country. The consumer correspondent of a radio program argued that the public should not hurry to follow the recommendation, and gave a reason. Which of the following reasons is NOT suited to be the correspondent's?
options: The owner of the newspaper in which the report appeared also owns a chain of supermarkets that competes with "Everyday"
The survey was conducted by a research company that has business dealings with "Everyday"
To know which chain is the cheapest one must compare prices over time, not rely on shoppers' impressions
Shopping at "Everyday" is indeed cheaper than at other chains, but so is the quality of what it sells
items.explanation: A newspaper owner who competes with "Everyday" would have reason to suppress the recommendation, not to publish it — the fact gives no ground to doubt it. (2) questions the survey's independence, (3) its method, (4) the conclusion drawn from it.
items.trust: derived-from-real-exam; 27 of 420 spot-checked against NITE keys, all correct

items.stem: In an essay on children's literature it was written: "Good children's literature does make use of the familiar conventions of society, and in doing so it helps children to understand the world; but it also knows not to be bound by them. The classic 'Grandfather Teodor,' for instance, is full of figures who keep the rules of their village to the letter, yet its whole purpose is to set off against them the singularity of the grandfather — eccentric, unruly, and loved by children precisely for that." According to the author of the essay, the figure of Grandfather Teodor —
options: helps the young reader to build a picture of the world by demonstrating conventions familiar to him
is marked by faults that children are meant to learn to avoid, though these faults are what make the book enjoyable
plays a central part in the book by helping the other figures to break with the conventions they keep
breaks the conventions of society, and stands out against the many figures in the book who keep them
items.explanation: The grandfather is the "not bound by them" half of the claim, and the rule-keeping figures exist to set him off. (1) gives him the other figures' role; (2) moralizes what the passage celebrates; (3) invents an influence on the other figures.
items.trust: derived-from-real-exam; 27 of 420 spot-checked against NITE keys, all correct

items.stem: In many species of plants the seeds lie dormant before they sprout. In dormancy their metabolism falls to a minimum, they lose no water, and they are able to withstand drought. A dormant seed sprouts only when its dormancy "breaks." In most species the breaking of dormancy is not synchronized: seeds formed in the same year may sprout in different years. Which of the following describes a synchronized breaking of dormancy in a species of plant?
options: All the seeds formed in a given year were dormant for the same number of years
Not all the seeds that came out of dormancy in a given year were formed in the same year
Seeds formed in a given year came out of dormancy in different years
All the seeds formed in a given year entered dormancy at the same time
items.explanation: Synchronized breaking means seeds of one year sprout together, hence equal dormancies. (3) is the unsynchronized case described; (2) concerns the year of formation, not of breaking; (4) concerns entering dormancy, not leaving it.
items.trust: derived-from-real-exam; 27 of 420 spot-checked against NITE keys, all correct

items.stem: In an article on nutrition it was written: "Lycopene, the substance that gives tomatoes their red color, is regarded as the most effective antioxidant in the carotenoid family — a family of molecules that neutralize free radicals. Studies have found that regular consumption of tomatoes is associated with a lower risk of certain diseases, and it is possible that lycopene is the cause. It cannot be ruled out, however, that other substances in the tomato, vitamin C among them, contribute to the beneficial effect." Which of the following claims is presented in the article as an established fact?
options: Molecules belonging to the carotenoid family neutralize free radicals
Regular consumption of tomatoes prevents certain diseases
Lycopene is the most effective antioxidant in the carotenoid family
Vitamin C contributes to the beneficial effect of eating tomatoes
items.explanation: (2) is what studies "found" as an association, not prevention; (3) is "regarded as"; (4) "cannot be ruled out." Only the definition of the family is asserted outright.
items.trust: derived-from-real-exam; 27 of 420 spot-checked against NITE keys, all correct

items.stem: Scholars of the philosopher Arben are divided over his conception of the purpose of human life. One school holds that in his principal work Arben claims that the purpose of man is the perfection of the intellect — that is, knowledge of the ultimate truth — but that this is a purpose man can never fully attain, since the limits of his intellect do not permit it. According to the other school, Arben held that although the purpose of man cannot be attained, man is obliged to strive toward it as far as he is able. Which of the following claims is correct according to the passage?
options: Scholars of both schools agree that, according to Arben, man cannot fully attain the purpose of his life
The scholars disagree about what, according to Arben, the purpose of human life is
The two schools differ over the question of what the full attainment of the purpose would consist in
The scholars disagree over whether, according to Arben, the human intellect can enable man to attain his purpose
items.explanation: Both schools say the purpose is unattainable; they differ over what follows from that — nothing about the purpose itself (2), its content (3), or the intellect's capacity (4).
items.trust: derived-from-real-exam; 27 of 420 spot-checked against NITE keys, all correct

items.stem: Researchers at a university hospital found that the hair follicles in the scalps of bald men contain no fewer stem cells than the follicles of men with a full head of hair. The cells in the bald scalps, however, do not function: they fail to develop into the progenitor cells from which a hair grows. Since 2007 the researchers have been seeking a way to make these cells resume their development. Which of the following headlines is best suited to a report of the study?
options: "Hair Restored: Experiments Show the Number of Progenitor Cells Can Be Increased"
"Mystery Solved: Bald Men Lose Their Follicles"
"Circle Closed: The Follicles of Bald Men Lack Stem Cells"
"Hope for the Bald? If the Cells Can Be Made to Develop, Hair May Return"
items.explanation: (1) reports a success the passage does not claim; (2) and (3) contradict the finding that the follicles and their stem cells are present.
items.trust: derived-from-real-exam; 27 of 420 spot-checked against NITE keys, all correct

items.stem: The minister of tourism recently announced that the state would give financial support to anyone who builds a new hotel in an area that has no hotel but is in demand among tourists. In a newspaper column criticizing the announcement, the columnist argued that the plan rests on a mistake. Which of the following claims is most likely to be the columnist's?
options: The very fact that no hotel has been built in an area is the clearest sign that tourists do not want to stay there
There is no need to build hotels in new areas, since the country already has more hotels than it needs
There is no justification for encouraging new hotels while the existing ones are losing money
The minister's task is to promote tourism by many means, and not by financial support alone
items.explanation: The plan assumes areas that are "in demand but without a hotel" exist; (1) denies exactly that. (2), (3) and (4) object to the plan without touching its premise.
items.trust: derived-from-real-exam; 27 of 420 spot-checked against NITE keys, all correct

items.stem: In an article on professional ethics it was written: "Psychologists employed in organizations such as the school system are in a position of dual loyalty. As psychologists they are bound first of all to the welfare of the person they treat, but as employees of the organization they are also bound to its interests. This position is liable to impair the psychologist's professional judgment." Which of the following claims is implied by the passage?
options: In a position of dual loyalty the professional judgment of the psychologist is necessarily impaired
The needs of the person treated do not always coincide with the interests of the organization that employs the psychologist
A psychologist employed by an organization ought to be bound first of all to the organization's interests
In practice, only psychologists employed in the school system find themselves in a position of dual loyalty
items.explanation: A loyalty can be dual only where the two claims can conflict. (1) turns "liable to" into "necessarily"; (3) reverses the stated order of duties; (4) turns an example into the only case.
items.trust: derived-from-real-exam; 27 of 420 spot-checked against NITE keys, all correct

items.stem: In an article on the medicine of a mountain tribe it was written: "When the healer of the tribe treated a sick person, he used both supernatural means — charms and incantations — and physiological treatments, such as herbs, bloodletting and the application of leeches. This combination of magical means with physiological treatment may seem puzzling, but in the eyes of the tribe it was entirely reasonable. In their view, an illness might be the work of demons or the result of natural causes, and since no one could know for certain which of the two was responsible for a given illness, it was best to fight it on both fronts at once." According to the passage, what did the members of the tribe believe?
options: The means at the healer's disposal enabled him to treat an illness, but not to know for certain what had caused it
The combination of magical and physiological means was strange, but it preserved a medical tradition worth keeping
The healer did not know which of his means would cure an illness of demonic origin and which an illness of natural origin
No illness could be cured by physiological means alone, and therefore the two kinds of means had to be combined
items.explanation: The tribe's reasoning turns on ignorance of the cause, not of the remedy: (3) misplaces the uncertainty; (2) and (4) supply grounds the passage does not give.
items.trust: derived-from-real-exam; 27 of 420 spot-checked against NITE keys, all correct

items.stem: Dr. Avi Elizur wrote: "Psychoanalysis teaches that understanding the adult depends on understanding the child he once was; and the historical sociologist claims that to understand a society today one must understand the social conventions it formed in the past. Therefore, ____." Which of the following best completes the passage?
options: understanding a person's past is a condition for understanding his present, and the same holds for a society
the makers of history are, like every person, shaped by their childhood
societies, like people, must learn the conventions that govern their conduct
understanding the adult requires examining the social conventions absorbed in his childhood
items.explanation: The two claims share one form — past as a condition of present — and the conclusion states it for both. (4) is the earlier error of chaining the two claims into one; (2) and (3) mix their subjects.
items.trust: derived-from-real-exam; 27 of 420 spot-checked against NITE keys, all correct

items.stem: The sculptor Michelangelo created his "David" in the years 1501–1504. The statue presents a figure that was much favored by the sculptors of the Renaissance — David the king — and has been regarded since its own day as a masterpiece; it is the emblem of Renaissance art in general and of Florence in particular, and millions of visitors come to the city each year to see it. Which of the following claims emerges from the passage?
options: During the Renaissance many sculptures depicting David were created
The Renaissance is regarded as the period in which art reached its peak
The importance attributed to the "David" today is greater than the importance attributed to it in the Renaissance
The most important work of art of the Renaissance is Michelangelo's "David"
items.explanation: "A figure much favored by the sculptors of the Renaissance" implies many depictions; (2) and (4) overreach; (3) is contradicted by "since its own day."
items.trust: derived-from-real-exam; 27 of 420 spot-checked against NITE keys, all correct

items.stem: One of the main purposes of punishing offenders is to deter others from similar offenses. ____. This, for example, is what the case before us teaches, which took place in England in the nineteenth century: a pickpocket was sentenced to death, and as was the custom the town crier summoned the public to come and watch the hanging. And behold — at the very moment when the crowd stood watching the pickpocket being hanged before their eyes, the pickpockets among them were busy at work. Which of the following sentences best completes the passage?
options: But no punishment, however severe, can deter would-be offenders unless it is made public
It seems reasonable to think that the more severe the punishment and the more people who witness it, the greater its deterrent effect; but this logic does not always survive the test of practice
But this was not always so: in the past punishment was regarded as the necessary revenge of society upon the offender, and deterrence was only a by-product of the wish to punish in public
It turns out, however, that precisely when the punishment is too severe, it may fail to deter and instead arouse sympathy for the offender
items.explanation: The example shows a severe, public punishment failing to deter — which is what (2) predicts; (1) makes publicity the missing ingredient although the hanging was public; (3) is a digression; (4) predicts sympathy the example does not show.
items.trust: derived-from-real-exam; 27 of 420 spot-checked against NITE keys, all correct

items.stem: Over the past thirty years a steady rise in temperatures has been recorded in all regions of the country. In the coastal region, however, the minimum temperatures have risen at a faster rate than the maximum temperatures, whereas in the mountain regions the maximum temperatures have risen faster than the minimum temperatures. Which of the following claims follows from the passage?
options: In the coastal region the minimum temperatures are rising, whereas in the mountain regions the maximum temperatures are rising
The minimum temperatures in the coastal region are rising faster than the minimum temperatures in the mountain regions
In the mountain regions the minimum temperatures are rising more slowly than the maximum temperatures
The minimum temperatures in the coastal region are rising faster than the maximum temperatures in the mountain regions
items.explanation: The passage compares minimum with maximum within each region; it licenses no comparison between regions — (2) and (4) — and (1) denies the rise that all temperatures share.

items.stem: Professor Hopkins wrote: "According to the biblical account, the first steps of the people of Israel on the stage of history were shaped by years of drought: drought drove Abraham to migrate to Canaan and, later, to go down to Egypt. In the course of the wandering in the desert, drought was the instrument by which the Lord punished the people, and the leaders in every generation used years of drought to warn the people against forsaking the covenant." What is the main subject of the passage?
options: The part played by rain and its absence in the history of the people of Israel
The factors that caused the people of Israel to leave Canaan
The means by which the leaders of the people of Israel governed them
The first steps of the people of Israel on the stage of history
items.explanation: Every sentence turns on drought; (2), (3) and (4) each name a part of the passage as if it were the whole.

items.stem: When Darwin published "On the Origin of Species" in 1859, the absence of fossils of "intermediate forms" — creatures with the features of two groups of animals — was regarded as one of the theory's principal weaknesses. Two years later, however, the fossil of Archaeopteryx, a creature with the features of both a dinosaur and a bird, was discovered, and it was seen as evidence of the descent of birds from dinosaurs. Which of the following claims follows from the passage?
options: When it was published, Darwin's theory was regarded as weak because it did not deal with intermediate forms
Darwin held that birds are descended from dinosaurs
The discovery of Archaeopteryx contributed to strengthening Darwin's theory
Until the discovery of Archaeopteryx, Darwin's theory was accepted by few
items.explanation: A weakness was the lack of a kind of evidence; the fossil supplied it. (1) confuses not dealing with a subject with lacking evidence for it; (2) and (4) go beyond the passage.

reading_comprehension.passage:
Many people believe that regular physical exercise improves a person's emotional state. In recent decades numerous studies have attempted to verify this belief, and their findings confirm that a connection exists; but, to the considerable surprise of the researchers, the connection turned out to be a weak one. In Denmark, for example, membership of sports clubs doubled in the course of the 1990s, yet the level of well-being that Danes reported in the same period did not rise in most cases, and even where a rise was recorded, it proved to be temporary. Similar results were obtained in Canada and in Japan, in surveys that followed tens of thousands of participants over several years.

Why does exercise exert so limited and so transient an influence on well-being? "Reference-point theory" can supply part of the answer. Its central claim is that people evaluate their condition primarily by comparing themselves with those around them, so that their well-being is determined first of all by how fit they are relative to others, rather than by their fitness in itself. According to the "peer hypothesis," which forms part of the theory, the more people regard others as their equals, the more they compare themselves with them; a person is unlikely to measure himself against a professional athlete, but very likely to measure himself against a colleague of his own age. This may explain why an improvement in fitness barely affects well-being. Shortly after a person joins a club, the group with which he compares himself changes: it now consists of the experienced members who train alongside him, and most of them are fitter than he is. His fitness has improved, but his position relative to his new reference group has, if anything, deteriorated.

An alternative explanation attributes the phenomenon to habituation. According to this view, people rapidly become accustomed to an improvement in their condition and soon regard it as a matter of course. Habituation raises the standard that a person expects of himself, and his expectations advance in step with his achievements, so that the distance between the two — which is what determines his satisfaction — remains approximately constant. A runner who once celebrated completing five kilometers will, within a few months, be dissatisfied with anything less than ten. The two explanations are not mutually exclusive, and several researchers have proposed that they operate simultaneously: comparison determines how a person evaluates his achievement at any given moment, while habituation determines how long the evaluation endures.

A study conducted in the Netherlands in 2014 attempted to distinguish between the two explanations. Its participants, none of whom had exercised regularly before, joined clubs and were followed for two years. Half of them trained in groups, and half trained alone with a personal instructor, so that the second half had no fellow members with whom to compare themselves. If comparison were the whole explanation, the participants who trained alone should have reported a lasting improvement in well-being; in fact their improvement faded almost as quickly as that of the others. The researchers concluded that habituation accounts for most of the phenomenon, and comparison for the remainder — though they conceded that a participant training alone may compare himself with acquaintances outside the club, so that the distinction between the two groups was less clean than they had intended.

Whatever the mechanism, the practical conclusion is the same, and it has been drawn by the promoters of public health with some reluctance: exercise is to be recommended for its physical benefits, which are well established, and not for its emotional ones, which are not. As the proverb has it: "Who is strong? He who is content with his strength."
reading_comprehension.glossary: transient — passing, short-lived; habituation — becoming accustomed to something; in step with — at the same pace as; mutually exclusive — unable to be true at the same time; reluctance — unwillingness.

reading_comprehension.passage:
For a long time scholars of literature assumed that the question of what makes a text a poem admits of a definite answer. According to the classical view, a poem is defined by a fixed set of characteristics, so that for any text one can determine, without hesitation, whether it is a poem or not. The model for such a determination was the sonnet: a sonnet has fourteen lines, and no text of fourteen lines fails to be a sonnet on that account, while no text of thirteen qualifies. The classical scholars believed that the category of the poem in general could be defined with the same precision, provided that its characteristics were correctly enumerated, and they devoted considerable effort to enumerating them.

This view has attracted extensive criticism. First, the critics argued, the boundaries between the categories of texts are not sharp at all. Where exactly, for example, does the boundary between prose and poetry lie? Can one point to a text that is prose but not yet poetry — a text on one side of the boundary, with its nearest neighbor on the other? The critics maintained that no such boundary can be located, and that the categories shade into one another by imperceptible degrees. Second, they argued, even where characteristics can be enumerated, they are not all necessary. The classical definition of a poem, for instance, appeared to require that a poem rhyme, that it maintain a regular meter, that it be divided into lines, and that it concern the emotions. Yet a text that does not rhyme, maintains no meter, runs continuously as a single line, and concerns a bicycle is nevertheless recognized as a poem by every competent reader.

The scholar Ruth Aviram proposed a different account of how readers classify texts. In her view we do not decide whether a text is a poem by checking it against a list of necessary characteristics, but by comparing it with a "model" — a typical, familiar example of the category. When we classify a text, we set it beside the model, and if it resembles the model sufficiently we count it as a poem; the more it resembles the model, the more readily we do so, and the less it resembles the model, the more we hesitate. Aviram's account explains what the classical view could not: why readers agree about the central cases and disagree about the marginal ones, and why a text can be "more of a poem" than another without either being excluded from the category. It also accommodates the sonnet, which had been the classical scholars' favorite illustration: a sonnet is simply a category whose model is unusually specific, so that resemblance to it is unusually easy to assess. Experimental evidence has subsequently supported the account. When readers were presented with unfamiliar texts and asked to classify them, their responses to the central examples were rapid and unanimous, whereas their responses to the marginal examples were slow, hesitant and inconsistent — precisely the pattern that classification by resemblance predicts and classification by enumeration does not.

Aviram's proposal has not gone unchallenged. Its critics have observed that the model itself must be selected by some criterion, and that the criterion, whatever it is, reintroduces the definition that the proposal was meant to dispense with. Aviram's reply was that the model is not selected at all but acquired: a reader learns what a poem is from the poems he encounters first, and his model is simply the residue of that encounter. This reply, however, raises a further difficulty, since readers whose first encounters differ should then possess different models and classify texts differently — which, as far as anyone has been able to determine, they do not.
reading_comprehension.glossary: admits of — allows for; enumerated — listed one by one; imperceptible — too small to be noticed; competent — properly qualified; residue — what remains after the rest has gone.

reading_comprehension.passage:
Between the seventeenth and the nineteenth centuries, the governments of Europe undertook the careful mapping of their territories. Surveyors were dispatched into the mountains to fix the positions and heights of passes, summits and springs. The methods of surveying available at the time were limited, however, and one of them in particular produced error after error, as the surveyors themselves were the first to admit. The consequences were serious. Roads were constructed at gradients that no vehicle could climb; bridges were designed for valleys whose depth had been misjudged; and more than one expedition, relying on a map that placed a pass a thousand feet lower than its true elevation, perished among the ridges.

The landscape that a surveyor observes in high mountains is virtually the same wherever he stands, summit succeeding summit to the horizon. Surveyors therefore relied on two measurements: the horizontal distance from a known point, and the elevation above sea level. The first of these could be measured with reasonable precision, and the surveyors of the period took pride in the accuracy they achieved. Using a chain and a carefully measured baseline, and observing the angles from either end of the baseline to the summit, a surveyor could calculate the distance to a point he was unable to reach. The elevation could not be determined in a similar way. In the mountains nothing within the surveyor's field of vision stands at a known height: the horizon itself is inclined by the slopes, and every summit is measured against neighboring summits whose elevations are as uncertain as its own. Surveyors were therefore obliged to rely on a chain of measurements ascending from the coast, in which a minor inaccuracy at each stage accumulated into a large one by the summit.

It had long been recognized that elevation can be calculated from atmospheric pressure, which diminishes as one ascends. For every hundred meters of ascent, the reading of a barometer decreases by about one unit. All that is required is to compare the reading obtained on the mountain with the reading recorded, at the same moment, at a station of known elevation. The obstacle lay in the instrument. The barometers of the period consisted of a column of mercury in a glass tube. Such an instrument could not be transported up a mountainside without spilling or shattering, and its readings fluctuated with the temperature, so that the comparison with the station's reading was of little value. Several expeditions nevertheless carried mercury barometers into the Alps, and the elevations they published for the same summit differed from one another by hundreds of meters, so that a map compiled from them was worse than no map at all.

The absence of a reliable method troubled France in particular. Its Alpine frontier was the most contested in Europe, and its military engineers required accurate maps of every pass through which an army might advance. In 1826 the Academy of Sciences in Paris announced a prize for a portable barometer of proven reliability. The prize was awarded to the instrument-maker Lucien Vidi, who had proposed to dispense with mercury altogether. His "aneroid" barometer measured the pressure by means of the expansion and contraction of a sealed metal capsule from which the air had been evacuated. The capsule neither spilled nor shattered, and it was almost insensible to cold, so that its reading on the mountain could be compared with the station's reading with confidence. Within a generation the elevations of the principal ranges of Europe had been established by survey parties equipped with Vidi's instrument, the discrepancies between rival maps had been settled, and the maps compiled from the new measurements remained in use, with only minor corrections, for a century.
reading_comprehension.glossary: cartography — map-making; negotiate (a gradient) — to travel up or down it; inclined — sloping; accumulated — built up gradually; evacuated — emptied of air; insensible to — unaffected by.

reading_comprehension.passage:
One of the great unresolved questions of biology is why human beings laugh. Laughter appears in every culture, begins in infancy, and seems to serve no obvious purpose. Until recently the accepted view was that laughter's principal function is the discharge of tension: laughing reduces the body's physiological stress and enables it to recover from strain. This view rests on numerous findings. In a study conducted at the University of Bern, two groups of participants were required to perform a stressful task; afterwards one group watched a comedy and the other a documentary about glaciers. The concentration of stress hormones measured in the comedy group declined more rapidly than in the other group. Dozens of similar studies, conducted with different tasks and different measures, report a reduction of approximately 15 percent in various indicators of stress following laughter, and the finding has been regarded as one of the most reliable in the field.

Recently the researcher Miriam Adler proposed an alternative explanation. The effect of laughter on stress, as documented in the studies, is small — too small, in her opinion, to be regarded as the principal function of a behavior so universal. She argues, moreover, that laughter is not necessary for the discharge of tension at all: if it were, every social animal would need to laugh, whereas numerous species never laugh and recover from strain no less efficiently than we do. She also reinterprets a well-known experiment from the 1970s, in which volunteers confined for two weeks in isolation, without company and therefore without laughter, exhibited a sharp rise in stress. The cause, she argues, was not the absence of laughter but the isolation itself. A recent experiment supports her interpretation: volunteers kept in company but prevented from laughing for a month — an instruction they reported as irksome but manageable — exhibited no rise in stress whatsoever, and their physiological measurements remained indistinguishable from those of a control group permitted to laugh freely.

In order to understand laughter, Adler maintains, one must examine not the body but the group — the circumstances in which each species lives. This approach, she claims, accounts for the considerable differences in laughter between individuals and between species. Why, for instance, do people laugh thirty times more frequently in company than alone, and why do they laugh most readily at remarks that are not amusing at all? Because, according to Adler, laughter is a signal transmitted to others: it informs the group that the individual laughing is at ease and intends no harm, and it thereby reduces the likelihood of conflict and spares the members of the group the effort of vigilance. "Within a group, the optimal strategy for an individual who wishes to retain his place is to laugh whenever he is not occupied with something more important," she writes. "Laughter is a kind of flag of truce." The apes that laugh most are those that live in the largest groups, in which quarrels are most frequent and most costly; and among human infants, laughter is directed almost exclusively at the caregivers on whose goodwill the infant depends, and appears only when the infant is old enough to distinguish them from strangers. Adler regards both observations as evidence that laughter is calibrated to the audience rather than to the state of the individual who laughs.

Adler's theory is now being tested by means of a new instrument: a miniature recorder, worn on the collar, that registers every laugh over a period of weeks together with an indication of whether anyone else was present. If the theory is correct, laughter in solitude should prove to be as rare as a flag raised in an empty field. Whether it is, the recordings will reveal.
reading_comprehension.glossary: discharge — release; universal — found everywhere; reinterprets — explains in a new way; vigilance — watchfulness; optimal — best possible.

questions.stem: Which assumption is necessary in order to conclude from the findings of the Bern study (lines 5–8) that laughter assists the discharge of tension?
options: Laughter is essential to the body's recovery from strain
The participants who watched the comedy were better at recovering from stress than those who watched the documentary
The task the participants performed was difficult
There was no difference between the two groups in their basic capacity to recover from stress
questions.explanation: The inference from the difference between the groups to the effect of the comedy requires that the groups were alike beforehand. (2) is the finding; (1) is the conclusion; (3) is not required.

questions.stem: From Adler's words in the second paragraph it arises that, in her view, the difference between the results of the experiment of the 1970s and those of the recent experiment stems from —
options: the different durations of the two experiments
the different conditions in which the volunteers were kept in each of the experiments
differences between the volunteers of the two experiments in their capacity to recover from stress
the fact that laughter was prevented in only one of the experiments
questions.explanation: Isolation in one, company in the other. (4) is false — laughter was absent in both; (1) and (3) are not what she says.

questions.stem: Which of the following graphs could represent the results of the two experiments described in the second paragraph? (Horizontal axis: time without laughter. Vertical axis: level of stress. Solid line: the experiment of the 1970s. Dashed line: the recent experiment.)
options: Solid line rising steeply; dashed line flat and low
Solid line flat and low; dashed line rising steeply
Solid line rising; dashed line falling
Solid line rising and then falling; dashed line flat and low
questions.explanation: A sharp rise in the one, no rise in the other.

questions.stem: Which of the following explanations could be offered, by Adler's school, for the fact that the members of a certain tribe living in the rain forest laugh far less than other people?
options: The members of the tribe are unusually adept at recovering from strain
The members of the tribe spend most of the day in tasks that leave no time for laughter
The members of the tribe live in small family groups in which quarrels are rare
The tribe's language contains no word for laughter
questions.explanation: Laughter, for Adler, is a signal whose value lies in preventing conflict within the group; where the group is small and conflict rare, the signal is little needed. (1) belongs to the theory she rejects; (2) and (4) are not explanations from the group's circumstances.

questions.stem: According to the third paragraph, how would Adler rank the following activities of a group member according to their contribution to retaining his place in the group?
options: Attending to something more important → laughing → vigilance
Laughing → attending to something more important → vigilance
Attending to something more important → vigilance → laughing
Vigilance → laughing → attending to something more important
questions.explanation: One laughs "whenever he is not occupied with something more important," so the important thing precedes laughter; and laughter "spares the effort of vigilance," so vigilance is what laughter replaces.

questions.stem: What is the structure of the passage?
options: A question → a possible answer → criticism of the answer → an alternative answer → a forthcoming test of the alternative answer
A question → an explanation → difficulties with the explanation → an alternative explanation → difficulties with the alternative explanation
A question → a research hypothesis → confirmation of the hypothesis → a further study → a further research question
A question → two possible answers → a study that permits a decision between them → the decision in favor of one of the answers
questions.explanation: The final paragraph describes a test not yet completed, so (2) and (4) exceed the passage; (3) omits the criticism that is its core.

reading_comprehension.passage:
In 1904 the draining of a peat bog near the Danish village of Hjortlund uncovered a wooden chest containing some six hundred thin wooden tablets. A discovery of this kind is exceptional. Wood survives from antiquity only where air cannot reach it, and the bog, which had submerged the tablets in acidic water for two thousand years, had preserved them. The preservation, however, had come at a considerable price. The tablets had been inscribed by cutting fine marks into their surface with a stylus, and in the course of two millennia the marks had contracted until they were barely perceptible. When the first tablets were lifted from the bog and dried, moreover, the wood warped and split. Most of what had been inscribed on those tablets was irretrievably lost. The tablets are virtually the only documents of the northern Iron Age composed by its inhabitants themselves rather than about them by Roman observers, and this accounts for the extraordinary efforts that have been devoted to deciphering them.

The development of infrared photography in the twentieth century revived the hope of reading the tablets. Infrared photography is sensitive to the composition of a surface. Different substances reflect infrared radiation in different proportions; a substance that reflects little appears dark in the photograph, and one that reflects much appears light. Since the ink employed on ancient documents was usually manufactured from soot, which reflects almost no infrared radiation, writing that has faded to invisibility in ordinary light frequently stands out with remarkable clarity in an infrared photograph. In recent decades this technique has recovered the text of faded parchments discovered in Egypt and in the Judean desert, and of manuscripts damaged by fire in European libraries, and scholars anticipated that it would accomplish the same for the tablets of Hjortlund.

The marks on the tablets of Hjortlund, however, had been cut into the wood rather than written upon it; no ink whatsoever had been used. The surface of a mark and the surface of the wood adjacent to it were therefore the same substance. They reflected infrared radiation in precisely the same proportion, and in an infrared photograph the two were indistinguishable. The technique that had proved so effective elsewhere was, for these particular tablets, entirely useless, and after a series of disappointing trials in the 1960s the attempt was abandoned. The tablets were returned to storage in sealed containers of water, and for half a century the chest of Hjortlund was regarded as a treasure that could be preserved but never read.

Then, in 2019, a team from the University of Aarhus succeeded in reading several of the tablets by means of a technique known as RTI. RTI likewise depends on photography, but it registers a different property of the surface: not its composition but its relief. The tablet is photographed dozens of times in succession, illuminated on each occasion from a different direction. A computer then combines the photographs into a single image. In this image every ridge and every hollow, however shallow, casts a shadow that shifts with the direction of the light. The technique had been developed for the study of coins and seals, whose designs are worn but not erased; its application to the tablets was proposed by a graduate student who had noticed that the marks, though invisible, could be felt with a fingertip. A mark cut into the wood, although it reflects light exactly as the surrounding wood does, is a hollow — and in the combined image its edges emerge as shadows. Reading a single tablet in this manner requires several days, and the team has so far recovered only a few dozen lines. It is confident, nevertheless, that the technique will eventually yield the contents of the entire chest.
reading_comprehension.glossary: submerged — kept under water; irretrievably — beyond recovery; anticipated — expected; adjacent — next to; relief — the raised and hollowed shape of a surface.

questions.stem: According to the first paragraph, which of the following is NOT correct regarding the tablets of Hjortlund?
options: They were inscribed by cutting marks into the wood
They warped and split in 1904
They were discovered in a place that air could not reach
They are documents composed by the inhabitants of the northern Iron Age themselves
questions.explanation: In 1904 they were discovered; the splitting occurred when they were dried afterward, and the contraction of the marks took place in the bog over two millennia. (1), (3) and (4) are each stated.

questions.stem: According to the second paragraph, why did the development of infrared photography revive the hope of reading the tablets?
options: Because infrared photography can identify the substances of which the tablets are composed, and so date them
Because infrared photography can read marks whose position on a tablet is already known
Because infrared photography can make faded writing visible
Because infrared photography can dry the tablets without splitting them
questions.explanation: The paragraph's central sentence. (1), (2) and (4) are not what the technique does.

questions.stem: Which of the following claims is NOT correct regarding the "faded parchments" mentioned in line 20?
options: They were composed in the same period as the tablets of Hjortlund
Some of them were discovered in the Judean desert
They were written in an ink that reflects less infrared radiation than the parchment does
Their text was recovered by means of infrared photography
questions.type: NOT correct about a secondary item — the unstated claim
questions.explanation: Their date is never given. (2) and (4) are stated; (3) follows from "soot, which reflects almost no infrared radiation."

questions.stem: According to the third paragraph, why was infrared photography useless for the tablets of Hjortlund?
options: Because too much time had elapsed between the making of the marks and the development of the technique
Because the marks had been made by cutting, so that they and the adjacent wood were the same substance
Because the proportion of infrared radiation the wood reflects is too small to be photographed
Because the difference between the wood and the marks in the radiation they reflect is too great
questions.explanation: No difference in composition, hence no difference in reflection. (4) is the opposite; (1) and (3) are not stated.

questions.stem: According to the last paragraph, which of the following sentences correctly describes the difference between infrared photography and RTI?
options: Infrared photography registers the composition of a surface, whereas RTI registers its relief
RTI, unlike infrared photography, cannot distinguish a soot-based ink from the surface on which it lies
Infrared photography registers the light a surface reflects, whereas RTI registers the light it absorbs
RTI, unlike infrared photography, distinguishes between two substances even when they reflect light in the same proportion
questions.explanation: "Not its composition but its relief." (4) makes RTI distinguish substances, which it does not; (2) and (3) are not stated.

questions.stem: According to the last paragraph, what occurred in 2019?
options: The technique RTI was invented
Researchers read a few dozen lines of the tablets of Hjortlund by means of RTI
A property of light previously unknown was discovered
A team of researchers succeeded in reading the entire contents of the chest
questions.explanation: (1) and (3) are not stated; (4) is what the team anticipates.

reading_comprehension.passage:
It is natural to assume that a young songbird acquires its song from the adult birds it hears around it. The song a bird produces as an adult is, after all, the characteristic song of its own species. This assumption, however, does not accord well with the well-documented fact that young birds produce phrases they have never heard. This difficulty has occupied a prominent position in the study of birdsong for more than sixty years. It is, in miniature, the same difficulty that confronts the student of human language, and the two disciplines have borrowed their arguments from each other repeatedly and productively.

The modern study of the subject originated in the critical review that the zoologist William Thorpe published in 1958 of the earlier accounts, which had attributed the acquisition of song to imitation alone. Thorpe distinguished between two kinds of input that a young bird may receive, which he called "exposure" and "feedback." Exposure consists in hearing the adult song. Feedback consists in information that a phrase the young bird has sung is defective. According to Thorpe, exposure by itself cannot teach a bird the rules by which the phrases of its species' song are combined. Since adult birds scarcely ever respond to a young bird's errors, the bird's knowledge must have an additional source. Thorpe designated this source the "song template." The template, in his conception, is an innate mechanism in the bird's brain that contains the rules common to the songs of all songbirds. The bird draws on it when it produces phrases it has never heard. The hypothesis was attractive because it accounted, at a stroke, for the two facts that imitation alone could not reconcile: the fidelity of the adult song to the species, and the novelty of the phrases in the young bird's repertoire.

Although Thorpe's approach gained widespread acceptance, evidence has accumulated over the past few decades that undermines its assumptions. It transpires, for instance, that adult birds do supply feedback, but indirectly. An adult female that hears a young male sing responds with a brief, characteristic fluttering of the wings. She flutters in the majority of cases in which the phrase was well formed, and in only a small minority of the cases in which it was not, so that the response itself can indicate an error. Other studies have found that the more frequently a phrase is sung in a young bird's surroundings, the earlier it appears in the young bird's own repertoire. Young birds raised in silence, by contrast, sing as adults a song so impoverished and monotonous that it barely qualifies as the song of their species. These findings underlie the "practice-based" school. It explains the acquisition of song comprehensively by general capacities of learning that every bird possesses — imitation, trial, and generalization from examples — and does not require the assumption of a template.

Criticism of Thorpe's theory has also arrived from another direction: the assumption that there exist rules common to the songs of all species, on which the "song template" depends, has proved exceptionally difficult to confirm. No such rule has been identified. Moreover, even the terminology employed to describe the rules — "syllable," for instance, or "refrain" — is derived predominantly from the study of the songbirds of Europe, and in many cases corresponds poorly to the songs of birds elsewhere at all. An ornithologist who attempted to describe the songs of the Australian lyrebird in these terms reported that the attempt produced a description of European birds rather than of the bird before him. Whether universal rules of song exist therefore remains an open question. So long as it remains open, the practice-based school has not prevailed, since it too has yet to demonstrate that general capacities of learning are sufficient.
reading_comprehension.glossary: accord with — agree with; defective — faulty; innate — present from birth; transpires — turns out; impoverished — poor, lacking.

questions.stem: Which of the following claims best summarizes the "difficulty" (line 4)?
options: A young bird's knowledge of song apparently rests only on the phrases it has heard, and yet it can produce new phrases
There are apparently phrases that young birds hear only rarely, and yet their knowledge rests on them
A young bird's knowledge of song apparently rests on the song of its own species, and yet it sometimes produces phrases that violate its rules
Young birds are apparently able to produce phrases they have never heard, and yet the song they sing as adults is the song of their species
questions.explanation: The tension is between learning from what is heard and producing what was not. (3) makes the new phrases defective; (2) and (4) rearrange the facts without the tension.

questions.stem: According to Thorpe's approach, why must the bird's knowledge "have an additional source" (line 14)?
options: Because almost all the input a young bird receives is exposure, and exposure is insufficient for learning the rules of the song
Because the feedback a young bird receives prevents it from making use of exposure
Because young birds hear too few adult songs to learn the rules from them
Because correcting a young bird's error cannot teach it the rule it violated
questions.explanation: Two premises — exposure cannot suffice, feedback is almost absent — and the conclusion. (3) makes the input too scarce rather than the wrong kind; (2) and (4) are not stated.

questions.stem: Which of the following is the best example of the "indirect" feedback described in lines 19–18?
options: A young bird sings a phrase, and an adult male drives it from the branch
A young bird sings a phrase, and an adult female sings the same phrase back to it in its correct form
A young bird sings a phrase, and an adult female flutters her wings
A young bird sings a phrase, and an adult male sings a different phrase
questions.explanation: The response is a signal, not a correction. (1) and (2) are direct responses to the error; (4) is not a response to it.

questions.stem: According to what is implied in the third paragraph, why can "the response itself … indicate an error" (line 24)?
options: Because adult females never respond to a young bird's well-formed phrases
Because if the young bird's phrase had been well formed, the female would have responded in the same manner
Because if the young bird's phrase had been defective, the probability that the female would respond is relatively small
Because adult females invariably respond to a young bird's defective phrases
questions.explanation: The asymmetry: response is probable after a good phrase and improbable after a defective one, so the absence of a response carries information. (1) and (4) convert "majority" and "small minority" into "never" and "invariably"; (2) removes the asymmetry.

questions.stem: In lines 29–23 it is written: "the 'practice-based' school … does not require the assumption of a template." What is the advantage of the practice-based school over Thorpe's approach?
options: It explains the acquisition of song comprehensively by general capacities of learning alone, and does not assume an additional mechanism, as Thorpe's approach does
Unlike Thorpe's approach, it is consistent with the finding that the more common a phrase is in a young bird's surroundings, the earlier the bird learns it
Unlike Thorpe's approach, it holds that general capacities of learning underlie imitation and generalization
It holds that several "song templates" participate in the acquisition of song, and does not assume a single template, as Thorpe's approach does
questions.explanation: Economy: no special mechanism. (4) multiplies the mechanism; (2) is a finding, not the advantage; (3) reverses the relation between capacities and imitation.

questions.stem: What is claimed in the last paragraph regarding terms such as "syllable" and "refrain"?
options: In practice, universal rules of song can be formulated without them
There are songbirds to whose songs they are not applicable at all
They no longer fit the description of the songs of the birds studied in Europe
They apply to the songs of all birds, but serve to formulate rules only for some
questions.explanation: "In many cases corresponds poorly to the songs of birds elsewhere at all." (3) reverses the geography; (1) and (4) are not stated.

reading_comprehension.passage:
The lagoon of Teremba, on the coast of Pacific Melanesia, supports a greater diversity of reef fish than any other body of water of comparable size, and the villages along its shore have subsisted on it for centuries. The lagoon is nevertheless in grave ecological danger, and its condition has been deteriorating continuously since the middle of the twentieth century. Because of the cyclones that devastated the region in those decades and the civil disturbances that followed independence, its predicament attracted comparatively little international attention. Only in the last decade have international organizations begun to investigate systematically what is occurring in the lagoon and to attempt to preserve what remains of its fish. Their preliminary surveys indicate that of the two hundred species recorded in the lagoon in the 1930s, approximately a third can no longer be found.

The marine biologist Solomon Tarai maintains that the principal cause of the decline is the rock grouper. This fish was introduced into the lagoon in the 1950s by officials of the colonial administration, who wished to provide the fishermen with a large fish to catch in place of the small reef bream on which the villages had always depended. The grouper, which may weigh eighty kilograms, indiscriminately consumes whatever is smaller than itself, and the bream — a small fish that grazes on the algae of the reef — is smaller than almost everything. Within twenty years the grouper had eaten the bream almost out of existence. Moreover, since the grouper inhabits the deep water at the center of the lagoon, beyond the operational range of the villagers' canoes, many of the fishermen were left with nothing whatever to catch. Those who persisted were compelled to travel to the reefs of neighboring islands, where they were unwelcome and where the catch was frequently confiscated.

Unlike the fishermen, the governments of the island states regard the grouper as an unqualified blessing. Its flesh commands high prices in the markets of Asia, and its export provides the states with a revenue they never previously possessed, and a significant proportion of their foreign currency. The vessels that harvest the grouper from the deep water belong to companies from overseas, as do the plants on the shore that clean and freeze the catch. The plants have transformed the villagers' livelihoods in ways that nobody planned. The women, for instance, who formerly purchased bream from the canoes, dried it in the sun and sold it inland, now purchase from the plants the parts of the grouper that the export trade rejects — the heads and the skeletons — dry them as they dried the bream, and sell them at the roadside. The trade is considerably smaller than it was, and its product is inferior; but it survives, and it remains in the same hands.

A further danger to the lagoon is the expansion of areas in which the water contains no oxygen and no organism survives. These areas, it was assumed, were also the grouper's doing. It had eaten the bream; the algae that the bream had grazed multiplied unchecked; the dead algae sank and decomposed; and the decomposition consumed the oxygen. The explanation was accepted unquestioningly for years, and it appeared in every report on the lagoon. But when a team from the University of the South Pacific extracted cores from the bed of the lagoon, the layers of sediment contradicted it. The dead areas had begun to expand before the grouper was ever introduced — in precisely the years in which sugar mills were constructed along the rivers that drain into the lagoon, and the mills began to discharge into the rivers the waste that nourishes algae, particularly the phosphates from the refining process. The grouper, it appears, has accelerated a process that human industry began.
reading_comprehension.glossary: subsisted on — lived from; predicament — difficult situation; commands (a price) — obtains; inferior — of lower quality; decomposed — rotted; accelerated — made faster.

questions.stem: Why are the "civil disturbances" (line 5) mentioned in the first paragraph?
options: To present the conditions in which the villagers of the lagoon live
To explain why the condition of the lagoon received proper attention only recently
Because they are among the dangers that threaten the lagoon
Because they mark the beginning of the lagoon's decline
questions.explanation: The disturbances, together with the cyclones, are the reason attention was directed elsewhere. (3) and (4) make them a cause of the decline; (1) is not their function.

questions.stem: Which of the following claims is implied by the third paragraph?
options: The plants constructed on the shore help, indirectly, to preserve part of the villagers' traditional way of life
The governments of the island states cooperate with companies from overseas
The increase in the states' revenue from the grouper has increased the fishermen's income
The fishermen of the villages sell their catch to the plants on the shore
questions.explanation: The women dry and sell the grouper's skeletons as they dried and sold the bream — the trade survives in altered form, "in the same hands." (2) is not stated; (3) and (4) contradict the passage.

questions.stem: According to the explanation described in lines 31–26, what is the order of events that led to the "further danger"?
options: The grouper multiplies → the bream is eaten out → the algae multiply → the dead areas expand
The algae multiply → the dead areas expand → the bream is eaten out → the grouper multiplies
The grouper multiplies → the dead areas expand → the bream is eaten out → the algae multiply
The algae multiply → the grouper multiplies → the dead areas expand → the bream is eaten out
questions.explanation: The chain as the passage states it.

questions.stem: Suppose a new species of fish were introduced into the lagoon, and that within a few years the condition of the lagoon and of the villages on its shore improved considerably. Which of the following fish is best suited to be that species?
options: A fish that may weigh fifty kilograms, and feeds on the rock grouper and on the reef bream
A fish that lives near the shore, grazes on algae, and is not prey to other fish
A fish that may weigh seventy kilograms, lives in the deep water, and feeds on algae
A fish that lives near the shore, feeds on small fish, and is not prey to other fish
questions.type: applying the passage to a hypothetical
questions.explanation: It performs the bream's function (algae), within range of the canoes (shore), and survives the grouper (not prey). (1) and (4) consume what should be preserved; (3) lives where the villagers cannot fish.

questions.stem: According to the last paragraph, what did the sediment cores reveal?
options: That the dead areas had begun to expand before the grouper was introduced
That the grouper had not eaten the bream out of existence
That the algae in the lagoon do not decompose
That the sugar mills were constructed after the grouper was introduced
questions.explanation: The timing is the whole finding. (4) reverses it; (2) and (3) contradict the passage.

questions.stem: Following their studies, Tarai and the team from the University of the South Pacific publish a joint article presenting their shared conclusions. Which of the following titles is best suited to it?
options: The lagoon of Teremba: the destructive effects of the rock grouper
The lagoon of Teremba: an uncontrolled fishery and its social and economic effects
The lagoon of Teremba: the ecological consequences of an introduced species
The lagoon of Teremba: natural processes and human influence
questions.type: a title for a joint work
questions.explanation: Tarai's cause is the grouper; the team's is the mills — only a title that holds both is shared. (1) and (3) are Tarai alone; (2) is neither.
