reading_comprehension.passage:
Every animal requires food, and almost all the food on land derives, at one remove or another, from plants; but the plants themselves depend on something considerably less conspicuous. Before a plant can utilize the minerals in the soil, dead organic matter must be decomposed and its minerals released, and this is the indispensable function of the soil's bacteria. The process, which proceeds invisibly and continuously beneath every field and forest, is the first link in the chain of fertility. The bacteria decompose leaves, wood and the bodies of animals; the minerals they release are absorbed by the roots of plants; and the plants in turn nourish the animals. The greater the bacterial population a soil contains, the more fertile it is.

Several environmental factors limit the abundance of soil bacteria and affect their distribution. Temperature is one of them: bacterial activity is almost completely suspended in frozen soil. Acidity is another, though only in unusual soils, such as those of peat bogs or of certain volcanic slopes, where it may suppress bacterial activity almost entirely. Salinity, similarly, suppresses bacteria in coastal soils and in irrigated fields where evaporation has concentrated the dissolved salts, but it is a local phenomenon rather than a general one.

The principal factor limiting bacteria in the soils of arid regions is moisture. Bacteria require water in order to be active, and require a steady supply of it in order to survive. The quantity of water in a soil determines not only how many bacteria inhabit it but also of what kinds. In soils that dry out for prolonged periods there are few bacteria, of exceptionally hardy varieties that revive rapidly and complete their work in the brief interval after rain. In humid regions, by contrast, bacteria are abundant and extraordinarily diverse, and there the principal factor limiting them is not water but the supply of dead organic matter to decompose.

In the soils of the humid tropics, however, the limiting factor is neither water nor organic matter, but minerals — principally potassium and phosphorus, which are comparatively scarce in most soils and are continuously consumed by the organisms that inhabit them. In the tropics the heavy rains carry the minerals downward, along with the fine particles of clay to which they adhere, into a layer of soil far beneath the roots. This layer is effectively inaccessible to the bacteria and to the roots, since almost all of them inhabit the topmost soil, the only layer that air penetrates. Because the minerals descend and do not ascend, the topmost soil is chronically deficient in them, and the forest that grows on it is poorer than its impressive dimensions would suggest. There are exceptions, however, wherever the deep soil is brought to the surface: on the mounds that termites construct from soil they carry up from far below, and in the fields of farmers who dig deep before planting. In such places, and only in such places, the soil is rich in minerals, and the crops that grow on it are renowned throughout the surrounding region. Agricultural scientists have attempted to reproduce the effect artificially by ploughing to a depth of two meters, but the expense has generally proved prohibitive.

The distribution of soil bacteria across the earth therefore exerts a profound and frequently underestimated influence on the distribution of all life, since it determines the fertility of the soil and, through it, the quantity of plant and animal life a region can sustain. Soil bacteria consequently rank among the most important living things in the ecological balance of the world — for the minerals they release are the foundation of every form of life on land.
reading_comprehension.glossary: conspicuous — easily noticed; decomposed — broken down, rotted; prolonged — lasting a long time; adhere — stick; deficient in — lacking; sustain — support.

questions.stem: What makes the soil's bacteria "the first link in the chain of fertility" (line 5)?
options: The fact that they release the minerals on which plants, and through them animals, depend
The fact that they decompose the bodies of animals
The fact that they are the most numerous living things in the soil
The fact that the more of them a soil contains, the more fertile it is
questions.explanation: The chain runs bacteria → minerals → plants → animals; (2) is only part of their function, (3) is not stated, (4) is a consequence.

questions.stem: According to the passage, which of the following claims explains why "in soils that dry out for prolonged periods there are few bacteria" (line 17)?
options: "Bacterial activity is almost completely suspended" in frozen soil (line 10)
Bacteria "require a steady supply of it in order to survive" (line 16)
The hardy kinds "complete their work in the brief interval after rain" (line 19)
"In humid regions … bacteria are abundant and extraordinarily diverse" (line 19)
questions.explanation: Few bacteria where the water is not steady, because a steady supply is what survival requires. (1) concerns temperature; (3) describes the survivors; (4) is the contrasting case.

questions.stem: Which of the following could replace the words "along with" (line 25) without changing the meaning of the sentence?
options: on top of
despite
by means of
together with
questions.explanation: The minerals descend in company with the clay to which they adhere. (3) would make the clay the instrument; (1) and (2) alter the relation.

questions.stem: What is "the surface" mentioned in line 29?
options: The mounds that termites construct
The fields of farmers
The topmost layer of the soil
The layer of soil far beneath the roots
questions.explanation: The deep soil is brought up to where roots and bacteria are — the topmost layer. (1) and (2) are the places where this occurs, not the surface itself; (4) is the opposite layer.

questions.stem: According to the passage, it is reasonable to find in ____ bacteria that are ____, since ____ is the principal factor limiting bacteria in those areas. Which of the following completes the sentence best?
options: frozen regions / of hardy kinds / temperature
the soils of the humid tropics / abundant / the supply of minerals
humid regions / diverse / the supply of dead organic matter
the fields of farmers / scarce / the depth of digging
questions.explanation: Humid regions: abundant and extraordinarily diverse, limited by organic matter. (1) transfers the arid regions' hardiness to frozen ground; (2) makes the tropics abundant, which the passage denies; (4) reverses the farmers' case.

questions.stem: According to the fourth paragraph, which of the following would apparently be the case if the rains of the tropics carried the minerals upward rather than downward?
options: The termites' mounds would no longer be richer in minerals than the surrounding soil
The bacteria of the tropics would inhabit the deep soil rather than the topmost layer
The clay particles would no longer adhere to the minerals
The forests of the tropics would be poorer than they are
questions.explanation: The mounds are rich only because they bring up what the rain carried down; if the rain carried it up, nothing would distinguish them. (2) contradicts "the only layer that air penetrates"; (3) is unrelated; (4) reverses the effect.

reading_comprehension.passage:
A handful of inventions are customarily credited with having changed the world — the printing press, the electric light, the computer. The barcode, first employed at a supermarket checkout in 1974, is not one of them. Unlike the great inventions, it involved no technological breakthrough whatever. It consists of nothing more than a sequence of black lines printed on a label, and the scanner that reads it was assembled from components that had existed for years. And yet its influence on our daily lives has been decisive. Economists who have attempted to quantify that influence estimate that the barcode has saved the retail trade of the industrialized countries several hundred billion dollars, and the estimate is probably conservative.

The fact that a cashier at the checkout does not enter the price of anything by hand seems to us today self-evident; but until the 1970s the pricing of merchandise was the most expensive and laborious component of selling it. Every item that arrived at a shop had to be marked with its price manually. Every sale had to be registered by a clerk reading the mark. Every inventory of the stock had to be compiled by clerks walking the shelves with lists, an operation that in a large shop occupied several employees for a week. A shop that stocked many kinds of merchandise required many clerks, and consequently most shops stocked few kinds; a grocer of the 1960s who carried more than a thousand distinct items was regarded as extravagant, and possibly reckless. The barcode replaced this entire apparatus with a single operation: the code printed on the item is read by a scanner, and the price, the sale and the inventory are recorded simultaneously, without a clerk touching a pen. The saving was immediate and enormous: within five years of the first installation, the labor expended on pricing in the supermarkets of the United States had diminished by two thirds.

The fundamental revolution, however, lay not in the barcode itself but in its standardization. For a scanner to read a code, every code must be constructed in the same manner; and for a code printed by a manufacturer in one country to be read in a shop in another, the manner must be identical throughout the world, and enforced by an authority that every manufacturer acknowledges. Establishing a universal standard acceptable to all the participants was a matter of dispute for years. The countries that had already begun to employ codes of their own were the losers, since a change of standard obliged them to replace every scanner and every label in use. Japan, for example, which had printed codes of eight digits on millions of items, was obliged to reprint them all with thirteen; and the manufacturers of scanners in the United States, whose machines read codes of twelve digits, were obliged to reconstruct them to read the additional digit that the rest of the world had adopted. The negotiations were conducted by committees of engineers, but their outcome was determined predominantly by the commercial weight of the participants, and the standard eventually adopted was, unsurprisingly, the one favored by the largest retailers.

Like many inventions, the barcode has not benefited everyone. Small shops that could not afford scanners lost their customers to the chains that could, and tens of thousands of them closed within a decade; in France alone, the number of independent grocers fell by half between 1975 and 1990; the clerks who had registered sales lost their employment permanently; and the record that the scanner retains of every purchase has generated persistent controversy about how much a retailer should know about the people who buy from it. Whether the gain is worth the cost is a matter of opinion. That the barcode matters is not.
reading_comprehension.glossary: customarily — usually; apparatus — system of procedures; simultaneously — at the same time; standardization — making everything conform to one standard; obliged — forced; retains — keeps.

questions.stem: The barcode "is not one of them" (line 2) — that is, it is NOT one of the inventions that —
options: people mistakenly believe involved a technological breakthrough
brought about great changes in human society
many people believe affected human society decisively
owe their importance to a technological or scientific breakthrough
questions.explanation: The following sentence supplies the reason: "unlike the great inventions, it involved no technological breakthrough." (2) and (3) contradict "its influence … has been decisive."

questions.stem: The sentence in line 5 is given below four times, each time with a different word stressed. Which of the stresses best expresses the sentence's intent in the passage?
options: The fact that a **cashier** at the checkout does not enter the price of anything by hand seems to us today self-evident
The fact that a cashier at the checkout does not **enter** the price of anything by hand seems to us today self-evident
The fact that a cashier at the checkout does not enter the **price** of anything by hand seems to us today self-evident
The fact that a cashier at the checkout does not enter the price of anything by hand seems to us **today** self-evident
questions.explanation: The sentence sets the present against the past that follows ("but until the 1970s…"); "today" carries the contrast.

questions.stem: According to the second paragraph, why did shops in the 1960s stock few kinds of merchandise?
options: Because in that period the cost of handling each kind of merchandise was high, so that stocking many kinds required many clerks
Because the differences between the prices of merchandise were small in every shop, so that customers had little reason to want variety
Because in that period the merchandise available to shops was limited, owing to the absence of a suitable industry
Because there were as yet no technologies for producing merchandise cheaply, and expensive merchandise sold slowly
questions.explanation: Pricing, registering and inventory were performed manually per item; more kinds meant more clerks. (2), (3) and (4) supply reasons the passage does not give.

questions.stem: According to the third paragraph, what would happen if each country established its own standard for the barcode?
options: It would be impossible to read codes by scanner
In many cases it would be more difficult to print codes on merchandise
In many cases merchandise printed with a code in one country could not be scanned in a shop in another
Scanners would have to be constructed to read codes of every length simultaneously
questions.type: what would happen without a standard
questions.explanation: "For a code printed by a manufacturer in one country to be read in a shop in another, the manner must be identical throughout the world, and enforced by an authority that every manufacturer acknowledges." (1) overstates; (2) and (4) are not stated.

questions.stem: According to the second and third paragraphs, in which of the following options are the events presented in the correct chronological order?
options: Merchandise was expensive for most people → the countries agreed on a universal standard → the barcode was invented → some countries had to replace their scanners
Pricing merchandise required much labor → the barcode came into use → some countries replaced their scanners and labels → the codes of the world became uniform

Shops stocked few kinds of merchandise → the barcode reduced pricing to a single operation → the countries agreed on a universal standard → some countries had to reprint labels and reconstruct scanners
Technological developments made merchandise cheap → shops stocked more kinds of merchandise → the barcode replaced the price mark → an international standard was established
questions.explanation: (1) places the standard before the invention; (2) places the countries' changes before the standard that compelled them; (4) invents a first step and reverses the second.

questions.stem: According to the last paragraph, on which of the following questions are opinions divided?
options: Whether the gain from the spread of the barcode outweighs the social harm and the harm to privacy it has caused
Whether the barcode is responsible for the harm the spread of the chains has caused, or whether that harm would have occurred without it
Whether the closing of small shops and the loss of the clerks' employment are the unavoidable consequences of the growth of the chains
Whether the harm the barcode has done to small shops justifies restricting its use by the chains
questions.explanation: "Whether the gain is worth the cost is a matter of opinion." (2), (3) and (4) are questions the passage does not raise.

reading_comprehension.trust: passage + question set; answers not verified against a NITE key

reading_comprehension.passage:
When the toy manufacturer Landor engaged the psychologist Ada Feld in 1991 to design the ideal doll, it anticipated a doll that every child would love. Feld, a specialist in children's play, tested dozens of prototypes on hundreds of children and asked them to rank the designs in order of preference. The results astonished the company's executives: there was no single doll that a majority of children preferred. Instead the children fell into three distinct groups — those who wanted a doll that resembled a baby, those who wanted one that resembled an adult, and those who wanted one that resembled nobody at all — and a prototype that pleased one group was emphatically rejected by the other two. The pursuit of a universal doll, Feld concluded, was misconceived, because no such doll exists. The company, which had invested heavily in the project, was reluctant to accept the conclusion, and commissioned two further studies before conceding that Feld was right.

Feld's conclusion has since been confirmed independently for numerous toys; but one toy is the exception: the teddy bear. Although manufacturers have attempted for a century to sell bears of various kinds, a single design satisfies almost everyone, irrespective of age, sex or nationality. The story begins in the 1900s, when stuffed toys were sold with eyes of glass mounted on wire pins, which worked loose and were occasionally swallowed by infants. In 1908 the child-welfare board of Nuremberg declared the pins a hazard, and the manufacturer Margarete Steiff replaced them with eyes embroidered in thread. The embroidered eyes could not be detached; but they also gave the bear a new face — round, close-set and level — and customers, it transpired, preferred it overwhelmingly. Within a few years every competing manufacturer had copied the design, and the Steiff bear became the standard from which no bear since has departed significantly. Manufacturers who experimented with alternatives — bears with elongated faces, bears with glass eyes restored, bears with painted smiles — abandoned them within a season.

Why does the bear satisfy everyone? One explanation, proposed by developmental psychologists, is that it possesses, in balance, all five of the characteristics to which small children respond in an object: it is soft to the touch, it can be held in both arms, its face is symmetrical, its eyes are large in proportion to its head, and its expression is neither happy nor sad. Most toys possess two or three of these characteristics. A doll with a laughing face has a fixed mood, which the child cannot alter to suit his own; a plastic animal, however appealing its proportions, cannot be embraced. The bear possesses all five, and none of them to excess. The explanation accounts for the failure of the experimental alternatives: each of them sacrificed one characteristic in the attempt to enhance another.

An alternative explanation invokes the tendency of small children to reject whatever is unfamiliar — unfamiliar food, unfamiliar places, unfamiliar people. This tendency presumably protected children in the past, when the unfamiliar was frequently dangerous; but today it chiefly obstructs them. Parents, however, have discovered a practical use for the bear. Taken along to the first day at nursery or to the doctor's waiting room, it converts an unfamiliar place into one that contains something familiar, and the child accepts what he would otherwise have refused. Nursery teachers report that the children who arrive with a bear settle within days, while those who arrive without one may take weeks. The bear, in other words, is not merely a toy but an instrument by which parents circumvent a tendency that evolution has left them unable to switch off.
reading_comprehension.glossary: engaged — hired; misconceived — based on a mistaken idea; hazard — danger; embroidered — sewn with thread; transpired — turned out; invokes — calls upon (as an explanation).

questions.stem: Roni and Michal heard Feld's conclusion and argued that their own preferences in board games could serve as evidence in its favor. Which of the following best describes Roni's and Michal's preferences?
options: Roni plays games of chance, whereas Michal prefers games of strategy, because they are cheaper
Roni prefers games that end within twenty minutes, whereas Michal maintains that a short game cannot be a good one
Roni and Michal agree that the game they play should have dice, but only Roni wants it to have cards as well
Roni and Michal both prefer games of strategy; Michal was doubtful at first, but now she agrees that strategy is what makes a game
questions.type: evidence that would support a claim
questions.explanation: Two players in different groups, one of whom rejects what the other prefers. (1) is a difference of price, not of taste; (3) is a difference of detail within agreement; (4) is a convergence.

questions.stem: Which of the following arises from the second paragraph regarding the Nuremberg board's ruling that the pins were a hazard (line 16)?
options: The ruling was subsequently found to be mistaken
The ruling led to the design of the bear known today
The ruling led to a prohibition on the sale of stuffed toys
The ruling was issued before the first stuffed toys were sold
questions.explanation: The embroidered eyes, adopted because of the ruling, gave the bear its face. (1), (3) and (4) are not stated.

questions.stem: According to the passage, which of the following completes the sentence below correctly? "The fact that the teddy bear ____ could strengthen ____."
options: with glass eyes was considered hazardous / the explanation that was accepted until 1991
that children prefer sells almost without competitors / Feld's conclusion
with a laughing face is scarcely sold today / Feld's conclusion
enjoys an unchallenged standing even today / the belief that was accepted until 1991
questions.explanation: Before Feld, the company believed in a universal toy; the bear's standing supports that belief. (2) and (3) offer a universal product as support for the conclusion that none exists; (1) links a fact about safety to a belief about taste.

questions.stem: According to the second paragraph, which of the following characteristics is NOT common to the bear with glass eyes and the bear sold today, but belongs to only one of them?
options: The eyes
Eyes embroidered in thread
Being a stuffed toy
Being sold to children
questions.explanation: The embroidered eyes are what the ruling introduced. (1), (3) and (4) belong to both.

questions.stem: Which of the following claims is implied by the last paragraph?
options: Parents of small children are insufficiently careful about keeping hazardous things from them
Parents begin taking their children to unfamiliar places only when the children are old enough for nursery
Today small children are rarely offered anything they do not already know
The tendency to reject the unfamiliar causes small children to reject things that are not dangerous
questions.explanation: The tendency protected once and "today chiefly obstructs them" — it now rejects what is harmless. (1), (2) and (3) are not implied.

questions.stem: Which of the following best summarizes the claims made in the passage?
options: Preferences in toys are universal; but there are a few toys about which children disagree; the bear is an example of a toy about which they agree, and the five characteristics explain why

Preferences in toys are generally not universal; in the case of the bear, however, the preference is universal; the five characteristics explain why the bear is so widely liked, and the rejection of the unfamiliar explains why small children in particular need it
Feld demonstrated that children differ in their preferences; in the past, for example, children loved two kinds of bear, and today they love one; the passage offers two explanations for the change

An experiment showed that preferences in toys are not universal; a further test found that the bear is an exception; children, and especially small children, tend to love toys that possess five characteristics
questions.explanation: Rule, exception, two explanations in their places. (1) reverses the rule; (3) invents a change over time; (4) converts the five characteristics into a general tendency.

reading_comprehension.passage:
Until the 1970s students of communication unanimously held that every gesture a person makes conveys information, and that it can therefore be accurate or inaccurate. This assumption was overturned by the publication of "Gesture and Action" by the anthropologist Adam Kendon. Kendon argued that the traditional view does not fit every kind of gesture. Gestures that describe a state of affairs — "descriptive gestures," in his terminology — can indeed be accurate or inaccurate. A hand held at knee height to indicate the height of a child either corresponds to the child's height or does not. But consider a hand raised in an auction room. This gesture describes nothing. It is not an attempt to convey a fact, and it therefore cannot be accurate or inaccurate. Rather, it makes a bid — it alters the state of affairs instead of reporting it. Gestures of this kind Kendon designated "active gestures." The distinction, he noted, cuts across the conventional classifications of gesture, since a single movement — a raised hand — may be descriptive in one situation and active in another.

According to Kendon, an active gesture cannot be accurate or inaccurate, but it can succeed or fail. In order to succeed, that is, to alter the state of affairs, it must satisfy what Kendon called "conditions of success." It must be made, for example, in a setting in which the convention on which it relies is in force, and it must be made by someone entitled to make it. A raised hand constitutes a bid only in an auction room, during the sale, by a person registered to bid. If a spectator raises his hand, or a bidder raises it after the hammer has fallen, the gesture alters nothing, however distinctly and deliberately it was made. A further condition is sincerity: a person who raises his hand in bid must intend to pay. Kendon observed that the conditions are seldom stated explicitly, and that people acquire them, as they acquire the conventions of their language, without deliberate instruction.

After Kendon had formulated the distinction between the two kinds of gesture, however, he came to reject it. He argued that the informational content of a gesture is insufficient to characterize it completely. Every gesture, according to Kendon, is composed of three layers: the **movement**, that is, the motion of the hand or the body itself; the **act** performed by means of the movement, such as pointing, requesting, warning or bidding; and the **effect** the gesture exerts on those who observe it, on their thoughts and on their subsequent conduct and decisions. It follows that every gesture is, in a sense, an active gesture, since every gesture performs some act. Kendon replaced the distinction between descriptive and active gestures with a distinction between explicit and implicit active gestures — gestures in which the act performed is immediately evident, and gestures in which it must be inferred from the circumstances.

To illustrate Kendon's method of analysis, consider the following illustration. At dinner, Dana wants the salt, which stands beside Yosi. She looks at Yosi and inclines her head toward the salt. The movement is the inclination of the head accompanied by the glance. The act performed is a request — the inclination is made in a setting in which Dana's plate is unsalted and Yosi is nearest to the salt, and this setting indicates what act the movement performs. The effect is whether Yosi passes the salt or does not. Dana's gesture is an implicit active gesture, and it corresponds to the explicit gesture of pointing at the salt and then at herself, which performs the same act by a movement whose meaning requires no setting to be understood. The analysis applies, Kendon maintained, to every gesture whatever, from the diplomatic handshake to the referee's whistle, and it is for this reason that his three layers have been adopted throughout the discipline.
reading_comprehension.glossary: conveys — communicates; terminology — set of technical terms; entitled — having the right; explicitly — in clear, direct words; inferred — worked out from indirect evidence; inclines — tilts.

questions.stem: According to the first paragraph, which of the following claims is correct regarding Kendon's book?
options: The study of active gestures had begun before it was published
It reinforced the explanation of gesture that was accepted among students of communication when it was published
It was published before the 1970s
It exerted a marked influence on the study of gesture
questions.explanation: "This assumption was overturned by the publication…" (1) and (3) are not stated; (2) is the opposite.

questions.stem: According to the first paragraph, which of the following gestures is an active gesture?
options: A hand held out flat to indicate the width of a table
A nod to confirm that the story a friend is telling is true
A shrug to indicate that one does not know the answer
A hand laid on a chair at a meeting to claim it as one's seat
questions.explanation: The hand on the chair alters the state of affairs — the seat is now taken; it reports nothing. (1), (2) and (3) convey information and can be accurate or inaccurate.

questions.stem: Which of the following factors is NOT mentioned in the second paragraph as a factor on which the success of an active gesture depends?
options: The setting in which the gesture is made
Whether the gesture is accurate or inaccurate
The sincerity of the person making the gesture
The identity of the person making the gesture
questions.explanation: Accuracy is precisely what the paragraph says active gestures cannot possess. (1), (3) and (4) are the three conditions.

questions.stem: According to the third paragraph, how does Kendon blur the distinction between active and descriptive gestures?
options: He determines that the two kinds of gesture do not exist at all
He argues that everything he originally defined as an active gesture is a descriptive gesture, and everything he originally defined as a descriptive gesture is an active gesture
He determines that all gestures are, in effect, active gestures
He demonstrates that a third kind of gesture exists in addition to the active and the descriptive
questions.explanation: "Every gesture is, in a sense, an active gesture." (2) reverses rather than blurs; (1) and (4) are not what he does.

questions.stem: According to the third paragraph, which of the following completes the sentence below best? "When a person makes a gesture, he employs ____ in order to achieve ____."
options: an effect / a movement that corresponds to the act
a movement / an effect that corresponds to the act
a movement / an act that corresponds to the effect
an act / an effect that corresponds to the movement
questions.explanation: The movement is the means, the act is what it performs, the effect is what is sought. (3) places the effect before the act; (1) and (4) reverse the means.

questions.stem: In lines 37–32 it is written: "this setting indicates what act the movement performs." What is "this setting"?
options: A situation in which Dana is having dinner with Yosi
A situation in which the subject of the conversation is the food
A situation in which Dana's plate is unsalted and Yosi is nearest to the salt
A situation in which Yosi may pass the salt or may not
questions.explanation: The setting that makes the inclination a request. (1) is the occasion, not the setting; (2) is not stated; (4) is the effect.

reading_comprehension.passage:
Pranayama is an ancient Indian method of treating illness by the regulation of the breath. According to the Indian tradition on which it draws, a vital force — prana — circulates in the body along channels called nadis. Illness, according to this doctrine, results from an obstruction or an imbalance in the circulation of prana, and the breathing exercises of pranayama are intended to clear the channels and restore the equilibrium. The exercises themselves are elaborate, and a full course of them may occupy an hour each day and requires months of instruction.

At the beginning of the twentieth century Indian teachers began to propagate pranayama in the West, and for some years it enjoyed a vogue in Europe and America, adopted by, among others, several prominent writers, at least two members of the British aristocracy, and a small number of physicians. In the 1930s, however, the vogue subsided, principally because of the increasing authority of Western medicine, which regarded pranayama as superstition. In the same years the standing of pranayama declined in India as well, under the influence of the medical schools the British had established there. It might have been forgotten altogether but for the independence of India in 1947, after which the new government promoted the traditional practices as part of the national heritage — and because they were inexpensive, and the new state could not afford Western medicine for a population of three hundred million. Nehru himself, who headed the government, did not believe in pranayama. "I have no faith in it," he wrote to a colleague, "but the people have, and we need them healthy."

It appears, then, that the fortunes of pranayama depended on social circumstances rather than on its efficacy. Whether it was practised in a given decade tells us what the decade thought of Indian tradition, and nothing whatever about whether the exercises work. In the 1970s Western medicine, which had dismissed it, began to subject it to controlled trials. Many of the trials detected an effect, and in 1978 the World Health Organization published a list of conditions — among them elevated blood pressure and asthma — for which breathing exercises were judged to be beneficial. The mechanism nevertheless remained a puzzle, since terms such as prana and nadis have no meaning in Western physiology. The trials could establish that patients who performed the exercises improved; they could not establish why, and the Organization's list was accordingly published with a note conceding that the mechanism was unknown.

Although Western science found no explanation for the therapeutic power of pranayama, a few scientific explanations of its capacity to reduce blood pressure were proposed. According to one, slow and deep breathing stimulates a nerve that runs from the brain to the heart and slows the heartbeat. But this explanation is also in doubt, since the slowing of the heartbeat persists for minutes only, whereas the reduction in blood pressure that the trials detected persisted for weeks. An effect that outlasts its supposed cause by such a margin, the critics observed, must have some other cause.

The doubt is not confined to the mechanism. Many scientists attribute the entire effect of pranayama to the placebo effect — the improvement that derives not from the treatment itself but from the patient's belief in it and his expectation of relief. If they are correct, the trials that detected an effect were defective, since a trial in which the patient knows that he is being treated cannot separate the treatment from his belief in it. How, then, did the World Health Organization accept them? The suspicion arises that the influence of India, which in those years led the bloc of non-aligned states, and from whose eyes the Organization wished to conceal its poor opinion of Indian medicine, played its part.
reading_comprehension.glossary: equilibrium — balance; propagate — spread; subsided — died down; efficacy — effectiveness; therapeutic — healing; defective — faulty.

questions.stem: According to the first paragraph, what are nadis?
options: The points at which prana enters the body
The breathing exercises of pranayama
The channels along which prana circulates in the body
The obstructions that cause illness
questions.explanation: (1), (2) and (4) are other elements of the doctrine.

questions.stem: Why is the independence of India (line 12) mentioned in the passage?
options: Because it is considered to have obstructed the advance of medicine in India
Because in its wake the standing of pranayama in India rose
Because the aspiration to revive the traditional practices was one of its causes
Because it led to the decline of pranayama in the West, as in India
questions.explanation: The revival is what followed it. (3) reverses cause and effect; (1) and (4) are not stated.

questions.stem: According to the third paragraph, which of the following statements reflects the position of Western medicine toward pranayama after the publication of the World Health Organization's list in 1978?
options: Although there is no obstacle to its use, further trials are required to test its efficacy
There are indeed conditions for which it may be beneficial, but it is not clear how it operates
The existence of prana and of nadis has indeed been demonstrated in trials, but it is doubtful whether they can be located in the body
Although trials have exposed its mechanism, it is doubtful whether it is an effective treatment
questions.explanation: Effect accepted, mechanism a puzzle. (3) and (4) reverse what was and was not found; (1) is not the position.

questions.stem: Which explanation is offered in the fourth paragraph for pranayama's capacity to reduce blood pressure?
options: During the exercises, air is inhaled that carries substances which reduce blood pressure
The breathing stimulates a nerve that slows the heartbeat
The exercises bring about the release of substances in the brain that relieve pain
The exercises lead to an improved circulation of prana in the body
questions.explanation: (4) is the traditional explanation the paragraph sets aside; (1) and (3) are not offered.

questions.stem: What arises from the last paragraph regarding the World Health Organization?
options: It presumably feared that the publication of the trials that tested pranayama would be interpreted in India as contempt for Indian tradition
It was prepared to conceal from the Indians the findings of trials that showed pranayama to have only a placebo effect
Its decision to support the use of pranayama, although the trials showed that it is ineffective, stemmed from a wish to please the Indians
Had it not been influenced by political considerations, it presumably would not have relied on the findings of the trials that found pranayama effective
questions.explanation: The paragraph's argument: the trials were defective, so their acceptance requires another explanation — the suspected political one. (3) says the trials showed no effect, which they did not; (1) and (2) are not stated.

questions.stem: What is the structure of the passage?
options: Presentation of pranayama → the differences between its standing in the West and in the East → the effect of Indian independence on its standing in the East → doubt about its effect in the scientific era

Presentation of pranayama → its uses in the East and the difficulty of Western medicine in accepting them → attempts by Western science to explain its mechanism → criticism of the World Health Organization's position toward it

Presentation of pranayama → social circumstances that affected its standing in the East and in the West → the attitude of Western science toward it → doubt about the credibility of the support the World Health Organization gave it

Presentation of pranayama → social circumstances that led to a change in its standing in the East and in the West → proof of the method's efficacy in the terms of Western medicine → proof that it is ineffective, and criticism of its foundations
questions.explanation: (4) claims proofs the passage does not provide; (2) omits the social history; (1) confines the circumstances to the East.

reading_comprehension.passage:
The biologist perceives in the floor of the deep sea a region of exceptionally sparse and peculiar life. The geologist perceives in it a plain of slowly accumulating sediment. The engineer perceives in it a place of crushing pressure and perpetual and unvarying cold. But the most conspicuous characteristic of the deep sea floor is its poverty of food, since it underlies all the phenomena that these specialists observe. In the absence of light nothing grows there, and every organism that inhabits it must subsist on what descends from above. The scarcity of food is therefore the critical factor, which determines more decisively than anything else the appearance of the deep sea floor and the ways of life of its inhabitants.

A distinction should be drawn between food that arrives distributed thinly and uniformly over a wide area and food that arrives concentrated in a single place. The first kind is the continuous, almost imperceptible drizzle of minute organic particles that sink from the surface. The second kind — the "food fall" — is the carcass of a large animal, a whale or a great fish, that sinks intact to the floor: enormous, infrequent, and entirely unpredictable. Most of the food that reaches the deep floor arrives in the second manner, and this imposes considerable hardship on the animals that live there. An animal that has grown, or reproduced, on one fall requires food in order to continue living; and in order to surmount the difficulty the animals of the deep floor have "adapted" to the conditions that the food falls create.

The irregularity of the food falls is both spatial and temporal. Spatially, a fall does not spread over a wide area but lands at a single point, and there is no predicting where the subsequent one will land. It may be said that the floor immediately surrounding a fall, a minute fraction of the whole, receives all the food. The animals of the deep floor respond to this in two ways. Some — those incapable of traveling far — congregate permanently at the few locations where food arrives steadily, in the vicinity of the vents of warm water on the floor, and live there in remarkably dense colonies. Others, which are capable of traveling, roam the empty plains between the vents, and when a fall lands they converge on it from considerable distances, reproduce on it, and disperse again when it has been consumed. The two strategies are not interchangeable: a colony animal transplanted to the plains starves, and a roaming animal confined to a vent ceases to reproduce.

As stated, there is irregularity in time as well. The interval between one fall and the next is not fixed, and years may elapse in which no fall whatever lands. The roaming animals must be prepared to reproduce on any fall they reach, since they may never reach another; but they do not reproduce on every fall. Reproduction is initiated only by a fall exceeding a certain magnitude — a quantity that varies with the region — a threshold — since the young require food for months after they hatch, and a small fall is consumed before they can mature. Moreover, the threshold is not uniform: it is higher in the emptiest basins than in the richer ones. In the emptiest basins a small fall is less likely than elsewhere to be followed by another before the young starve, and reproducing on it would be a wager with distinctly unfavorable prospects. Regarded in this way, the animals of the deep floor resemble a speculator who assesses, before every investment, the probability of a return, and a visitor to the deep might suppose that nature there is as calculating as the market. But that would be an illusion. The animals calculate nothing; natural selection has simply eliminated, invisibly and inexorably, over the generations, those that wagered on falls too small to repay them.
reading_comprehension.glossary: conspicuous — easily noticed; subsist on — live from; surmount — overcome; congregate — gather; interchangeable — able to be swapped; wager — bet.

questions.stem: Which of the following is NOT among "the phenomena that these specialists observe" (line 4)?
options: Sparse life
Slowly accumulating silt
Crushing pressure
Poverty of food
questions.explanation: The poverty of food "underlies" the phenomena; it is the cause, not one of them.

questions.stem: Which of the following claims CONTRADICTS what is stated in the second paragraph?
options: Food that reaches the deep floor does not, as a rule, arrive distributed over a wide area
Most of the food that reaches the deep floor arrives in falls
Food that arrives steadily makes life easier for the animals of the deep floor
Food that arrives concentrated in a single place arrives in small quantities
questions.explanation: The fall is "enormous." (1) and (2) restate the paragraph; (3) is consistent with "this imposes considerable hardship."

questions.stem: According to the third paragraph, in what do the animals incapable of traveling far differ from those capable of traveling?
options: The animals incapable of traveling far subsist on small quantities of food
The animals incapable of traveling far live mainly far from the vents of warm water
The animals capable of traveling can reproduce at locations where food arrives only rarely
The animals capable of traveling cannot live at locations where food arrives steadily
questions.explanation: The travelers reproduce on falls in the empty plains; the sedentary ones depend on steady food at the vents. (2) reverses the sedentary animals' habitat; (1) and (4) are not stated — a roaming animal confined to a vent lives, but does not reproduce.

questions.stem: Which of the following completes the sentence below best? "According to the last paragraph, in nature's exchange, ____ the stock exchange, ____."
options: as in / a loss means extinction
unlike / it does not matter when one invests
as in / the speculators assess the probability of success in advance
unlike / the speculator does not assess the probability at all
questions.explanation: "The animals calculate nothing" — the point at which the analogy fails. (3) is the illusion the passage rejects; (2) contradicts the threshold; (1) is not the contrast drawn.

questions.stem: According to the last paragraph, why is the reproduction threshold higher in the emptiest basins?
options: Because the falls that land in the emptiest basins are larger and harm the young
Because in the emptiest basins falls land in summer as well as in winter
Because in the emptiest basins the probability that one fall will soon be followed by another is especially low
Because only in the emptiest basins do the young require food after they hatch
questions.type: why a threshold rises with scarcity
questions.explanation: The probability of a subsequent fall sets the threshold. (4) makes a universal need local; (1) and (2) are not stated.

questions.stem: According to the third paragraph, what would happen to a colony animal transplanted to the empty plains?
options: It would converge on the next food fall from a great distance
It would starve
It would cease to reproduce but continue to live
It would establish a new colony at the nearest vent
questions.explanation: "A colony animal transplanted to the plains starves." (3) is the roaming animal's fate at a vent, reversed; (1) and (4) are not stated.

reading_comprehension.passage:
In 1861 the German scholar Hugo Bergmann published a study of the hymns of the Rigveda, the most ancient of the Indian scriptures, composed more than three thousand years ago. The most surprising of his numerous findings concerned smell. The hymns describe sacrifices, feasts and fields in considerable detail. Nevertheless they contain almost no words for smells. The smoke of the altar is "bitter," the flowers of the meadow are "sweet," the fat of the offering is "heavy." Moreover, the few words that do concern smell are employed in ways that appear to us thoroughly peculiar: the smell of fresh butter, for example, is described as "cold." Bergmann argued that these descriptions were composed by people whose sense of smell was less developed than ours. The reason for this, in his view, is that their sense of smell had not yet fully evolved.

Bergmann's claim was an audacious one: the theory of evolution, on which it depended, was still in its infancy, and the notion that a sense could develop over generations appeared distinctly far-fetched. But the claim was not abandoned. The philologist Otto Kranz undertook to investigate it a few years later. Kranz examined the words for smells in the oldest texts of many cultures. In the oldest of them the only words for smells are "foul" and "fragrant." In later texts words for particular smells appear — "smoky," "sour," "of meat." The last to appear, in every culture, are words for faint smells such as "musty" and "earthy." Kranz maintained that the order reflects a modification of the nose that occurred over the generations. He thereby went considerably further than Bergmann. The physiological component of his claim has since been abandoned; but the order of emergence he identified is still accepted, and it has been the point of departure of every subsequent investigation of the subject.

In the twentieth century anthropologists began to test the claim that the source of the phenomenon is physiological. They examined peoples whose languages possess comparatively few words for smells. Their preliminary findings appeared to support Bergmann and Kranz. All the languages possessed words for "foul" and "fragrant"; most possessed words for a few particular smells; and only some possessed words for faint smells. When a member of a people whose language had no word for "musty" was asked what an old cellar smells of, he answered "foul" or "of earth." The anthropologists then presented the members of such peoples with a set of scented papers and asked them to sort the papers by smell. They sorted the musty specimens apart from the foul and the earthy without the slightest hesitation. Their noses, evidently, distinguished what their vocabulary did not. The experiment has since been repeated with several unrelated languages, and the result has proved consistent: vocabulary constrains description, not discrimination.

Why, then, did they describe the cellar as foul or earthy? The linguist Asifa Majid explains it as follows: in a culture in which a smell has no name, it is entirely natural to assign it to a neighboring name — foul, for instance, or earthy — much as a person with no word for "turquoise" will call the color blue or green. If perception is not the issue, however, why the fixed order? Majid explains that as follows: since foulness is the smell of spoiled food, of sickness and of danger, every culture required a name for it urgently, and required it early. The faint smells, by contrast, seldom possessed comparable significance. A person can pass through life without ever needing to distinguish musty from earthy — and until people began to store grain and wine in cellars, the overwhelming majority did precisely that.
reading_comprehension.glossary: scriptures — sacred writings; peculiar — strange; audacious — bold, daring; philologist — scholar of languages and texts; modification — change; point of departure — starting point.

questions.stem: Which of the following best summarizes the findings of Bergmann's study described in the first paragraph?
options: In the hymns, words for smells sometimes describe things that do not smell as the words say, and this is especially marked in the use of the word "cold"
In the hymns, smells are described by words for tastes and textures, but words for smells are never used
In the hymns, things that we would describe by smell are described by other qualities, and the few words for smells are employed in unexpected ways
In the hymns, no words for smells appear at all, and the words for tastes do not always describe things that taste as they say
questions.explanation: Two findings, both retained: description by other qualities, and the peculiar use of the few smell words. (2) and (4) claim there are none; (1) confines the peculiarity to a single word.

questions.stem: Why is it noted in lines 9–10 that "the theory of evolution … was still in its infancy"?
options: To explain why Bergmann's claim was rejected for a long time
To explain how the scientific climate of the period influenced Bergmann's claim
To explain how the theory of evolution developed from studies such as Bergmann's
To explain why Bergmann's claim was an audacious one
questions.explanation: The remark follows "an audacious one" and supplies the reason. (1) contradicts "the claim was not abandoned"; (2) and (3) reverse the relation.

questions.stem: Which of the following descriptions fits both Bergmann's study and Kranz's study?
options: The study examined the texts of many cultures
The study examined ancient texts
The study concentrated on descriptions of faint smells
The study concentrated on the smell of fresh butter
questions.explanation: Bergmann examined one ancient corpus, Kranz the oldest texts of many cultures; (1), (3) and (4) belong to at most one study.

questions.stem: Which of the following best summarizes the findings described in the third paragraph regarding peoples whose languages have no word for "musty"?
options: They were able to identify the musty smell, but described it by the names of other smells
They could distinguish musty things from earthy ones only if the two were placed side by side
They could identify musty smells, but not faint smells in general
They could sort musty things from foul ones, but could not say which of the two the cellar smelled of
questions.explanation: Sorted apart without difficulty, named by a neighbor. (2) adds a condition; (3) and (4) are not what was found.

questions.stem: Why is the color "turquoise" mentioned in the last paragraph (line 34)?
options: To show that the naming of colors follows the same fixed order as the naming of smells
To illustrate how a quality without a name of its own is assigned to a neighboring name
To show that perception of colors, like perception of smells, depends on vocabulary
To present an example of a word that appeared late in the history of every language
questions.explanation: "Much as a person with no word for 'turquoise' will call the color blue or green" — an analogy for the assignment to a neighbor. (3) is the view the passage rejects; (1) and (4) are not claimed.

questions.stem: Which of the following claims is correct according to Majid's explanation of the fixed order in which words for smells emerge?
options: Had the smell of spoiled food been fragrant and foulness no indication of danger, foulness would presumably not have been named before the other smells
Had all fruit remained unripe, "sour" would presumably have been named before "foul"
Had the nose been able to distinguish faint smells before it could distinguish foulness, people would presumably have named the faint smells first
Had there been regions in which all food was stored in cellars, the languages that developed there would presumably have named "musty" before every other smell
questions.explanation: The priority of "foul" derives from what it signals; remove the signals and the priority disappears. (3) rests on perception, which Majid sets aside; (4) overreaches with "before every other"; (2) does not follow.

reading_comprehension.passage:
In excavations at the site of the ancient city of Meru, on the upper reaches of the river Sindh, clay tablets were uncovered bearing the earliest records of the kingdom of Meru, from the fourteenth century BCE. Scholars regard these tablets — the "vow tablets" — as having served in the rituals of the temple. The king vowed before the god an offering conditional upon a good harvest or a victory. The priests inscribed the vow on the tablet, and after the harvest or the battle the outcome was inscribed beside it, so that the tablet recorded both the undertaking and its fulfilment. The vow tablets constitute the oldest evidence of writing in the kingdom of Meru, and approximately four thousand of them have been recovered from the ruins of the temple precinct and its storerooms.

From the twelfth century BCE stone pillars have survived on which the kings of Meru had their achievements inscribed. The pillar inscriptions recount military campaigns, the construction of irrigation canals and donations to the temples. They were composed by officials of the royal household rather than by priests of the temple, but their purpose remained religious: the pillars stood in the courtyards of temples and were addressed to the gods. Unlike the vow tablets, the pillars record events retrospectively only. Their reliability as a record is questionable, since a king had no motive whatever to commemorate his defeats, and the campaigns they describe invariably conclude in victory, however improbable the victory may appear to a modern historian.

In the ninth century BCE the kingdom of Meru began to maintain records of a different kind — the "Registers of the Years," in which the events of each year were entered in a fixed sequence and in fixed formulas: the harvest, the flooding of the river, the campaigns, the deaths of nobles. The Registers constitute the earliest systematic record of events in the kingdom, and the most prominent example of this new practice. They record without explaining, however, so that a reader learns from them what occurred and not why it occurred. Their rigid adherence to the fixed sequence and formulas connects them to the tradition of the temple records from which they developed. So does the fact that they were maintained by officials of the court, in a chamber adjoining the royal archive.

Works of the kind of the Registers left a great deal unsaid, and in the eighth century BCE a new kind of writing arose in order to say it — the "Explanations," of which the best known is the Explanation of Tavar. The Explanations take the entries of the Registers and supply what the Registers omit. They give the causes of the events, the motives of the men who participated in them, and the connections between them. In the Explanation of Tavar the campaigns of the Registers become narratives, with reasons for their outbreak and lessons derived from their outcome. The Explanations were not regarded as replacing the Registers, and the two were copied and preserved together.

In the sixth century BCE the kingdom of Meru fragmented into rival principalities, and the writing of history became a weapon. Each principality maintained its own chronicle, composed by scribes in the service of its ruler, and each chronicle recounted the story of the kingdom's fragmentation so as to justify the claims of its own prince and discredit his rivals. The rigid sequence of the Registers gave way to narratives shaped by the requirements of the moment. A reader of the chronicles of two neighboring principalities could derive from them two histories that agreed on almost nothing. This continued until the fourth century BCE, when the prince of Tavar united the principalities under his rule. The new king terminated the rival chronicles: he closed the archives of the principalities and entrusted the writing of history to a college of officials of his own court, appointed for the purpose and answerable to him alone. They were to record the events of the kingdom, as the Registers had, in a fixed sequence and according to fixed rules.
reading_comprehension.glossary: retrospectively — after the event; commemorate — record in honor of; rigid — strict, unbending; fragmented — broke into pieces; discredit — damage the reputation of; terminated — put an end to.

questions.stem: A historian who studied the ancient kingdom of Meru observed: "The vow tablets served a double role in the rituals of the temple." What did the historian mean?
options: That the vow tablets served both to initiate the event and to record it
That the priests both inscribed the vows on the tablets and recited them before the god
That the vow tablets were both a religious instrument and a reliable record
That the vow tablets served both the kings of Meru and, in the twentieth century, the scholars who study them
questions.explanation: The vow was made by means of the tablet, and the outcome was inscribed on it. (2) and (4) are not roles in the ritual; (3) makes a claim about reliability the passage does not.

questions.stem: "The most prominent example of this new practice" (line 20) — that is, the most prominent example of —
options: the records that officials maintained in the temples
the events of the kingdom of Meru in the ninth century BCE
the vow tablets and the pillar inscriptions
the systematic recording of events
questions.explanation: The practice is the systematic record that the Registers inaugurated. (1) and (3) are the older kinds; (2) confuses the record with what it records.

questions.stem: According to the third paragraph, what does the Registers' rigid adherence to the fixed sequence and formulas testify to?
options: That the Registers were composed by the priests of the temple
That the Registers were addressed to the gods alone
That those who maintained the Registers continued, to some extent, the tradition of the temple records
That the Registers record important events only
questions.explanation: "Connect them to the tradition of the temple records from which they developed." (1) contradicts "officials of the court"; (2) and (4) are not stated.

questions.stem: "The connections between them" (line 28) — that is, between —
options: the events entered in the Registers and the documents on which the Explanations rely
the various events entered in the Registers
the events entered in the Registers and the events recounted in the Explanation of Tavar
the various events recounted in the Explanation of Tavar and not entered in the Registers
questions.explanation: The Explanations supply, for the entries of the Registers, the connections among those entries. (1), (3) and (4) introduce a second set that the sentence does not contain.

questions.stem: What is the central subject of the fourth paragraph?
options: The principal historical events of the kingdom of Meru in the eighth century BCE
The advantages and the shortcomings of the Explanation of Tavar as a historical record
The interests of the historians of Meru in the eighth century BCE
A method of recording that remedied a deficiency in the method that preceded it
questions.explanation: The Explanations supply what the Registers omit. (2) and (3) are not discussed; (1) is not the subject.

questions.stem: According to the last paragraph, how did the prince of Tavar terminate the rival chronicles?
options: He entrusted the writing of history to officials in his own service
He prohibited the study of the chronicles of the principalities
He created a stream of historical writing that contradicted the chronicles
He had the story of the kingdom's fragmentation written so as to justify his own claims
questions.explanation: The college of court officials, writing according to fixed rules. (2) is not what "closed the archives" states; (3) and (4) are what the princes had done.

reading_comprehension.source: Autumn 2022 §1 (a term whose everyday sense is corrected → the genre's most conspicuous feature, violation of accepted logic, with named examples → invented words and new meanings, with a quoted line → a graphic feature → the genre's real method: familiar signs deployed in unexpected ways; why adults find it harder than children → the closing question, is it children's literature, answered "not unequivocally")
reading_comprehension.passage:
The everyday interpretation of the term "nonsense" is words devoid of significance, or matters that are simply impossible. Those who occupy themselves with the literary genre bearing that name, however, do not regard its works as devoid of significance. Works of nonsense are not devoid of significance or of logic; they are founded on rules of their own, and a reader who fails to identify those rules will indeed find them unintelligible.

The most conspicuous characteristic of works of nonsense is a deliberate deviation from accepted logic, and an implied challenge to what is taken for granted. A celebrated illustration appears in "Alice in Wonderland," in which the March Hare offers the following argument: "You should say what you mean." "I do," Alice replies, "at least I mean what I say — that's the same thing, you know." "Not the same thing a bit!" says the Hare. The reasoning is founded on an entirely coherent principle — that reversing the order of a relation does not preserve it — and it is deployed against a proposition that everyone accepts without examination. The Hare, in other words, is not talking nonsense in the everyday sense at all; he is reasoning more rigorously than his interlocutor.

A further characteristic of works of nonsense is the invention of words and the assignment of new significations to existing ones. In the verse of Lea Goldberg, for instance, the speaker declares: "…a fool, a dolt, an utter clot / no letter and no line has got." A second illustration is the poem of Lewis Carroll named for the creature "Jabberwock," a word he invented. The poem employs invented words of good phonetic construction, and produces from them lines that a reader parses without in the least understanding. There are works of nonsense in which the invented words assume a still greater role, and the reader must infer their significations from the surrounding lines alone, as an archaeologist infers the meaning of an inscription from its context.

Certain works of nonsense possess a graphic characteristic as well: the words are arranged on the page so as to form a shape. In the poem of Morgenstern entitled "The Night Song of the Fish," the central portion of the composition consists entirely of two graphic symbols — a dash and an arc — arranged on the page in the shape of a fish. The reader who encounters it must decide whether he is reading a poem, contemplating a drawing, or doing both simultaneously. Morgenstern himself declined to say, and the composition has been reprinted in anthologies of poetry and in anthologies of graphic art alike.

Works of nonsense employ familiar signs, but combine them in unexpected and unaccustomed ways. The adult reader finds it difficult to interpret them, since he has already learned to read the world in a particular manner, and the boundaries of his imagination are consequently narrower. Children, by contrast, have not yet learned what may not be done, and they accept the invented word, the reversed relation and the fish composed of dashes without protest. Most of the adults who occupy themselves with a work of nonsense attempt to extract from it a coherent significance and are frustrated when they fail; children, who expect no such thing, are amused. The difference is not one of intelligence but of expectation.

It may be asked, accordingly, whether the literature of nonsense is a variety of children's literature. The answer is not unequivocal. There are works of nonsense that assist a child in learning the rules of language and of logic by violating them conspicuously, and thereby drawing attention to their existence. But there are works of nonsense that presuppose a reader who already knows the conventions intimately, since only such a reader can recognize precisely which convention is being violated. Works of that kind, although they employ the apparatus of children's literature, are addressed to adults.
reading_comprehension.glossary: devoid of — completely without; deliberate — intentional; phonetic — relating to speech sounds; parses — analyses the grammar of; unequivocal — admitting of only one interpretation; presuppose — assume in advance.

questions.stem: The expression whose significance is examined afresh in the verse of Lea Goldberg (lines 14–17) is —
options: human beings
an utter clot
a letter
a line
questions.explanation: "Clot" ordinarily denotes a fool; the verse revives its literal sense, so that a person with no letter and no line is one. (1), (3) and (4) are used in their ordinary senses.

questions.stem: "The reader must infer their significations from the surrounding lines" (line 20) — that is, more than in —
options: the model composed of two graphic symbols
other characteristics of nonsense
the poem of Carroll named for the Jabberwock
the verse of Lea Goldberg
questions.explanation: The sentence introduces works in which invented words assume "a still greater role" than in the case just described — Carroll's poem, whose invented words are parsed without being understood. (1) and (4) illustrate other characteristics.

questions.stem: The description of the fish-shaped arrangement of dashes and arcs (lines 23–28) is presented as an illustration of —
options: an interpretive possibility offered to children by "The Night Song of the Fish"
the single significance of a question in the work of Morgenstern
the manner in which adults interpret familiar signs in accustomed ways
a characteristic that pertains to the appearance of a work and not to its verbal content
questions.explanation: The graphic characteristic — the shape on the page. (3) is the adults' difficulty, discussed later; (1) and (2) are not what the example shows.

questions.stem: The words "It may be asked, accordingly" (line 37) refer to the fact that —
options: works of nonsense employ familiar signs
works of nonsense correspond to the world of language, of thought and of the imagination characteristic of children
adults derive pleasure from reading works of nonsense
the best way to teach children the rules of logic and of language is precisely by means of works of nonsense
questions.type: what a connective refers back to
questions.explanation: The preceding paragraph establishes that children accept what adults resist; the question about children's literature follows from it. (1) is a general feature; (3) contradicts the paragraph; (4) is a conclusion the passage does not draw.

questions.stem: According to the last paragraph, why does "the author" of certain works of nonsense require a reader who knows the conventions intimately?
options: So that adults may understand the work
So that the reader may recognize which convention is being violated
So as to convey a particular message by this means
Because his imagination governs his work
questions.explanation: "Only such a reader can recognize precisely which convention is being violated." (1) states the audience, not the reason; (3) and (4) are not stated.

questions.stem: What is the answer the passage gives to the question raised in the last paragraph?
options: The literature of nonsense is a variety of children's literature, since it assists children in learning the rules of language
The literature of nonsense is not a variety of children's literature, since it requires knowledge of the conventions
Some works of nonsense are addressed to children and some to adults
The question cannot be decided, since the boundaries of children's literature are themselves disputed
questions.explanation: "The answer is not unequivocal," followed by one kind of work of each sort. (1) and (2) take one half for the whole; (4) is not the reason given.
